stories.title: The preoperative window as a measurement and as a treatment
stories.premise: Preoperative treatment in this cell serves as an experiment at least as much as a treatment. Pathological complete response is rare here, which leaves nearly every endpoint read before surgery a proliferation measurement standing in for an outcome. Almost every question at this position turns on whether that substitution holds, and on whether a tumour's early response can be trusted to decide what happens after the operation.

chapters.title: Neoadjuvant therapy

questions.ask: Does the proliferation left after a short preoperative exposure measure how much a tumour depends on oestrogen?
questions.rationale: Oestrogen drives the cell cycle in this cell. The fraction of cells still dividing after a short exposure is therefore the most direct read-out of whether the drug is working. A pretreatment biopsy says how fast the tumour was growing. A biopsy taken on treatment says how much of that growth oestrogen was responsible for. CDK4/6 sits immediately downstream of the receptor. A tumour still proliferating on an aromatase inhibitor is the obvious place to put a cell-cycle drug.
questions.experiment: Paired biopsies taken before and during preoperative treatment, scored centrally for Ki67. The largest trial randomised a short perioperative course of an aromatase inhibitor against no perioperative treatment. Its primary endpoint was time to recurrence. The paired Ki67 was only a secondary objective. Another trial randomised the three aromatase inhibitors against each other. Smaller trials added a CDK4/6 inhibitor to an aromatase inhibitor, either as a randomised arm or as a within-patient step after an endocrine-only run-in. One ongoing trial profiles serial biopsies at single-cell resolution.
questions.finding: Endocrine therapy alone leaves a proliferating fraction in most tumours. How large that fraction is after the short exposure separates patients across a wide span of recurrence risk. The exposure itself changed no outcome. The three aromatase inhibitors are indistinguishable on this read-out. It reports the class and not the molecule. Adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor drives most tumours below the arrest threshold, far more of them than an aromatase inhibitor does alone. The arrest reverses once the drug is withdrawn.
questions.limitation: Complete cell cycle arrest is an assay threshold, not a biological state. The cut point was calibrated on tumours given endocrine therapy alone. It was built to grade endocrine dependence. A drug that stops the cycle whether or not the tumour depends on oestrogen crosses that line in nearly everyone, which is precisely what destroys its power to select. The thresholds in use are not even the same number from trial to trial. The within-patient designs also confound the added drug with longer time on treatment, because the second biopsy is both on more drug and later.
questions.next: If proliferation can be shut down almost completely, does that deeper suppression produce more of the tumour response a surgeon and a patient can see?

questions.ask: Does suppressing proliferation more deeply produce a better tumour response at surgery?
questions.rationale: Ki67 was adopted before surgery because it is quick, cheap and readable in a core biopsy. The whole case for using it rests on the assumption that it stands in for something the patient experiences. A drug that suppresses proliferation far more should therefore shrink tumours more, or leave less disease behind at operation. If it does neither, the surrogate and the outcome have come apart. The surrogate is then the thing to distrust.
questions.experiment: Trials that reported a proliferation endpoint and a clinical or pathological endpoint out of the same randomisation. One added a CDK4/6 inhibitor to letrozole and reported the change in Ki67 beside the clinical response rate. Another gave a short lead-in of the combination against an aromatase inhibitor alone, then operated on everyone who completed the preoperative course. Two more carried the combination through a full preoperative course against chemotherapy. One of those read residual cancer burden, pathological complete response and a composite prognostic index scored on the surgical specimen, the other a molecular risk score read on the same specimen. One trial asked directly whether early proliferation suppression converted into that composite index.
questions.finding: The proliferation endpoints separated the arms decisively. The clinical and pathological endpoints did not follow. Where both came out of one randomisation, a large difference in Ki67 sat beside a clinical response rate that was no different. In the comparison against chemotherapy the two arms changed places depending on which endpoint was read, chemotherapy ahead on residual disease and the combination ahead on the composite index. The trial that read a molecular risk score instead found the two arms level. Where early suppression was tested directly as a predictor of the composite index, it did not deliver one.
questions.limitation: Pathological complete response sits near its floor in this cell. A trial powered on it has almost no room to move. A null result there means very little. The composite index is not independent of the surrogate, because proliferation is one of its own components. A drug that suppresses proliferation therefore improves the index partly by construction. The molecular risk score is a reclassification of the tumour rather than a measure of what the patient gained at surgery. The trial that tested the translation most directly has conference and registry material behind it and no peer-reviewed report. Its negative result cannot be weighed as a published trial result.
questions.next: If pathological response cannot carry the argument in this cell, can the response measured during treatment still be used to decide who needs chemotherapy at all?

questions.ask: Can the tumour's response to preoperative treatment be used to withhold chemotherapy?
questions.rationale: Most of this cell gains little from cytotoxic treatment. The difficulty is telling who. A baseline genomic score infers endocrine dependence from the untreated tumour. A short preoperative course tests it instead. A tumour whose proliferation collapses under an aromatase inhibitor has demonstrated the dependence the score was trying to predict.
questions.experiment: Response-adapted designs: a short endocrine run-in, a central Ki67 read against a prespecified threshold, and a route to chemotherapy for the tumours that stay above it. One programme combined that window with a genomic score and tested whether the group given endocrine therapy alone was noninferior. Its successor randomises a CDK4/6 inhibitor against chemotherapy after the same kind of window, with invasive disease-free survival as the endpoint. Others dropped chemotherapy in favour of a CDK4/6 inhibitor and compared what was left at surgery, by molecular risk score or by cell-cycle arrest. One trial now recruiting carries the same idea through to distant metastasis-free survival.
questions.finding: Response does separate the population, and in the direction the biology predicts. Patients with an intermediate genomic score whose tumours responded in the window did as well as the control group whose score was low to begin with. Only a minority of tumours reach the endocrine-sensitive state these designs define, whichever endocrine drug is used to produce it. The trials that replaced chemotherapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor reached much the same molecular and proliferative state at surgery as chemotherapy did, at a lower cost in serious adverse events. The randomised trial that would settle the substitution on invasive disease-free survival has not reported.
questions.limitation: In the response-guided programme the groups were allocated by score and by response rather than by randomisation. The comparison is therefore between two differently selected populations and not between two ways of treating the same patient. Its window is preoperative. The therapy decision it drives is adjuvant. It does not test preoperative treatment at all. In the chemotherapy-replacement trials the arms produced similar estimates. Similar estimates are not noninferiority. None of those trials carried a noninferiority margin or the size to test one. The trial powered to show that endocrine and CDK4/6 treatment arrests the cycle in far more tumours than chemotherapy did not show it. It also randomised only the tumours whose proliferation stayed up after an endocrine run-in, a deliberately endocrine-resistant group and a small fraction of those registered. The whole family of designs turns on a Ki67 threshold that is read centrally in the trials and locally in clinic. The successor trial's own concordance analysis found that the two readings of one specimen do not always agree. The trial built to settle the question on distant control has published a design paper and nothing else. Nothing on its record is a result.
questions.next: If the endocrine backbone sets the ceiling on how many tumours respond, would a better receptor-directed drug raise it?

questions.ask: Does a better receptor-directed drug improve the tumour's early biological response more than an aromatase inhibitor?
questions.rationale: The first preoperative comparisons put an aromatase inhibitor against tamoxifen, in postmenopausal women and, with ovarian suppression, in premenopausal women. They are what established preoperative endocrine therapy as something worth doing at all. Changing between the aromatase inhibitors does not push the receptor axis any further, because they behave alike. Degrading the receptor rather than starving it should shut down more signalling. It should also keep working where the receptor is mutated.
questions.experiment: Short preoperative windows of two or four weeks, each ending in a central Ki67 score. One randomised an oral receptor degrader against anastrozole before putting both groups on the same combination. One randomised two doses of a second oral degrader against letrozole. One was a single arm read against an arrest threshold. Against these sit the older tamoxifen comparisons, which scored tumour size rather than proliferation, and a full-length preoperative phase III trial of an injectable degrader given alone and added to an aromatase inhibitor, with a prognostic composite scored at surgery.
questions.finding: The older comparisons did not all run one way. The aromatase inhibitor gave more tumour response than tamoxifen in the trial that established the approach, and again in premenopausal women treated with ovarian suppression. In two other preoperative comparisons the response rates were close and the difference was not significant. Among the newer agents, one oral degrader suppressed proliferation more than anastrozole over two weeks. The other matched letrozole without beating it. The single-arm study arrested the cycle in a minority of the tumours it treated. Over a full preoperative course the injectable degrader did not improve on an aromatase inhibitor on the trial's own prognostic endpoint, given alone or added to it.
questions.limitation: A window study is small because a short exposure is all its design asks for. Its endpoint is a ratio of two Ki67 scores. That ratio measures what the drug does to proliferation. It has never been shown to buy a lower recurrence rate. A better ratio is a better ratio and nothing more. The comparisons are also not on one footing. The older agent trials scored tumour response by callipers and by ultrasound. The two methods gave different response rates inside the same trial. One of those trials permitted concurrent chemotherapy, which contaminates the endocrine comparison. One window study stopped early for slow accrual. In another the primary comparison rests on the subset with paired central scores rather than on everyone randomised. The phase III trial enrolled a broader population and read a different endpoint entirely. It does not settle the window question. Neither do the window results overturn it.
questions.next: If the ceiling is not set by which receptor drug is given, is it set by the tumour's histology instead?

questions.ask: Does invasive lobular carcinoma need its own preoperative endocrine experiment?
questions.rationale: Lobular tumours lose E-cadherin and infiltrate in single files rather than forming a discrete mass. They are almost always receptor-positive and low grade. They respond poorly to cytotoxic treatment. Both halves of a neoadjuvant argument therefore change. Endocrine therapy becomes the plausible option rather than one of two. A tumour with no discrete mass cannot be measured by callipers or by imaging the way a ductal tumour can.
questions.experiment: A randomised short preoperative exposure to tamoxifen, to an aromatase inhibitor or to fulvestrant in lobular disease, read out as target engagement rather than as tumour response. Separately, a randomised preoperative trial of adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to endocrine therapy that enrolled receptor-positive disease of any histology, so that lobular and ductal tumours could be compared inside one trial.
questions.finding: Neither has reported the comparison it was built to make. The short-exposure study has conference and registry material only. Nothing on its record may be read as a published outcome. The only publication on the randomised trial's record is its axillary analysis, which found that clearing the axilla added nothing over sentinel node biopsy in node-positive disease after preoperative endocrine therapy.
questions.limitation: The short-exposure study is a phase zero design. It measures whether a drug reaches and engages its target. It cannot rank endocrine agents for efficacy. Reading it that way is the error its design invites. The randomised trial is named for lobular cancer but enrolled any histology. Lobular tumours were a minority of the patients in its published analysis. That report is a comparison inside a mixed population rather than a lobular trial. The endpoints of that publication are ones the paper itself calls prespecified exploratory. They say nothing about the trial's systemic question. No other trial at this position enrolled a lobular-only population. The histology argument rests on these two and on subgroups borrowed from elsewhere.
questions.next: If neither escalating the receptor drug nor separating the histology has raised the response, can a different mechanism raise it?

questions.ask: Can checkpoint blockade or an antibody-drug conjugate raise response where endocrine escalation has not?
questions.rationale: Luminal tumours are usually immunologically quiet. The high-grade, receptor-low end of this cell is not. An adaptive platform trial had already reported a pembrolizumab signal across HER2-negative disease rather than in triple-negative disease alone. Separately, most receptor-positive tumours express HER2 below the amplification threshold, which an antibody-drug conjugate can use as an address rather than as a driver.
questions.experiment: Two phase III trials added a checkpoint inhibitor to anthracycline and taxane-based preoperative chemotherapy in luminal disease, with pathological complete response as a primary endpoint and event-free survival to follow. Alongside them sit a randomised trial of preoperative radiation dose as an immune primer before checkpoint blockade, and a preoperative trial of an antibody-drug conjugate given with and without an aromatase inhibitor in receptor-positive, HER2-low disease rather than HER2-amplified disease. A single-arm study profiled what a CDK4/6 inhibitor on an endocrine backbone does to the immune and stromal compartments over a preoperative course.
questions.finding: Both phase III trials raised pathological complete response. In the one whose record reports the subgroup, the increase concentrated where PD-L1 was expressed. The event-free survival that decides whether the increase matters is immature where it has been reported at all. The profiling study found that a CDK4/6 inhibitor on an endocrine backbone diminished adaptive anti-tumour immunity, which is a reason to doubt that the two escalation strategies combine. The radiation-priming trial and the antibody-drug conjugate trial have conference and registry material only. Neither yet has a result to read.
questions.limitation: Pathological complete response is not the surrogate here that it is in triple-negative disease. A gain in it does not convert into an expectation about recurrence. One of the two phase III trials selected explicitly on grade, on low oestrogen receptor expression and on PD-L1, which is the end of this cell that behaves least like the rest of it. Its result does not generalise to the ordinary luminal tumour. The PD-L1 result there is scored with a single antibody clone against a single cut-off. A group defined by a marker is not a randomised comparison. The profiling study is single-arm. Its immune observation is a reason for doubt rather than a test of whether the strategies combine. The radiation-priming trial holds its receptor-positive and triple-negative cohorts separately. Nothing there may be read as a pooled population.
questions.next: Does a gain in pathological response, in a cell where pathological response is rare, convert into fewer distant recurrences?

stories.title: Choosing the intensity and the duration of endocrine treatment
stories.premise: Almost everyone in this cell is cured by local treatment and endocrine therapy, and the recurrences arrive over two decades rather than two years. So the adjuvant questions are not whether to treat but how hard, for how long, and for whom the extra years or the extra drug are worth their cost.

chapters.title: Adjuvant chemotherapy and the genomic assay decision
Adjuvant endocrine therapy
Adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibition

questions.ask: How completely does oestrogen have to be removed?
questions.rationale: Tamoxifen blocks the receptor; an aromatase inhibitor removes the ligand; ovarian suppression removes the source. Each step is a deeper intervention on the same axis, and each was expected to buy more disease control at more cost.
questions.experiment: Direct comparisons of an aromatase inhibitor against tamoxifen, and of ovarian suppression added to either, in premenopausal and postmenopausal populations separately.
questions.finding: Deeper suppression lowers recurrence, and the absolute gain tracks baseline risk rather than being uniform across the cell.
questions.limitation: None of these trials randomised the decision that a clinic actually makes, which is whether this particular patient's risk justifies the menopausal symptoms and the bone loss. Subgroup gradients are not the same as a randomised selection rule.
questions.next: If the benefit tracks risk, can risk be measured well enough to allocate the intensity rather than infer it after the fact?

questions.ask: How long should endocrine treatment continue?
questions.rationale: Recurrence in this cell continues at a roughly constant rate for at least twenty years, so treatment that stops at five years stops while the hazard is still running.
questions.experiment: Randomised extension beyond five years, in each of the sequences a clinic actually uses. Tamoxifen to ten years, an aromatase inhibitor after tamoxifen, an aromatase inhibitor after an aromatase inhibitor. Then, against the same question from the other side, trials of shorter or intermittent extension.
questions.finding: Extension lowers recurrence, the effect is smaller than the first five years bought, and several extension trials found that more was not better than less.
questions.limitation: The extension trials enrolled patients who had already tolerated five years, which is a selected population, and they differ in the drug taken first, so the results are not interchangeable across sequences.
questions.next: Since the benefit of extension is real but small, can the patients who get it be identified before ten years of treatment are prescribed to everyone?

questions.ask: Does adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy lower recurrence?
questions.rationale: CDK4/6 inhibition roughly doubles progression-free survival in metastatic hormone receptor-positive disease, and the cells that seed a late recurrence are the same lineage. If the drug works on macroscopic disease it should work on residual disease.
questions.experiment: Four trials added a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy, differing in the drug, the duration, and how high the enrolled risk was.
questions.finding: Two showed a durable improvement in invasive disease-free survival and two did not, and the split follows the specific drug, schedule and risk population rather than the class.
questions.limitation: These are not head-to-head trials. The populations, the treatment durations and the endpoints differ enough that the divergence cannot be attributed to the molecule alone. Overall survival has separated in one of the four. It is negative in one, immature in another and unreported in the last. The survival record therefore follows the same split the disease-free record does, and adds no independent evidence about which feature of these trials produced it.
questions.next: If escalation only pays at high risk, what is the risk threshold, and does it have to be measured before treatment or can it be read from the response to treatment?

questions.ask: Can the decision to give chemotherapy be made on biology rather than on anatomy?
questions.rationale: Node count and tumour size measure how long a cancer has been growing, not how much it depends on oestrogen. A genomic assay measures the second, which is what predicts whether cytotoxic treatment adds anything to endocrine treatment.
questions.experiment: Randomised trials that assigned chemotherapy by a genomic score rather than by stage, in node-negative and then node-positive disease, with survival as the endpoint.
questions.finding: A large fraction of this cell can omit chemotherapy without losing disease control, and the exceptions cluster by age and menopausal status rather than by score alone.
questions.limitation: The assays were validated on populations treated with the endocrine therapy of their era, and the age effect is confounded with ovarian function, so the benefit attributed to chemotherapy may partly be the benefit of chemotherapy-induced menopause.
questions.next: If a score taken once before treatment can allocate chemotherapy, can the tumour's own response to a short course of endocrine therapy allocate it better?

questions.ask: Can the response to treatment be used to allocate treatment, rather than the baseline alone?
questions.rationale: A baseline assay predicts; a short course of endocrine therapy tests. A tumour whose proliferation collapses under two weeks of an aromatase inhibitor has demonstrated the dependence the assay was trying to infer.
questions.experiment: Response-adapted designs that give a brief endocrine exposure, measure the change in proliferation, and route patients to chemotherapy or to endocrine treatment on what they see.
questions.finding: Response separates the population, and the endocrine-responsive group does well on endocrine treatment alone.
questions.limitation: A dynamic marker predicts outcome in a cohort that has already been selected on it, so the comparison is against a historical expectation rather than against the same patients treated the other way.
questions.next: Does adding CDK4/6 inhibition to the induction course change who looks responsive, and is that change real or an artefact of a drug that suppresses proliferation in everyone?

questions.ask: Does the choice of aromatase inhibitor, or the order it is given in, change the outcome?
questions.rationale: Three aromatase inhibitors reached the clinic within a few years of each other, and two of them are non-steroidal while the third is a steroidal inactivator. The mechanistic difference was expected to produce a clinical one. The separate question was whether five years of an inhibitor beats two or three years of tamoxifen followed by one.
questions.experiment: Head-to-head randomisation of one inhibitor against another in the adjuvant setting, and separately, randomisation of an upfront inhibitor against a planned switch from tamoxifen after two or three years.
questions.finding: No aromatase inhibitor beat another. The switch strategies that randomised patients already disease-free on tamoxifen improved outcomes over continuing it, while the trials that randomised the whole strategy from the start found upfront and switch approaches equivalent.
questions.limitation: The two designs are not comparable and are routinely read as though they were. A trial that randomises at two years enrols only patients who tolerated tamoxifen and did not relapse on it. That is a selected population, and its prognosis is better than that of the population randomised at diagnosis. The head-to-head agent trials were powered to show superiority and cannot establish equivalence.
questions.next: If the agent does not matter and the sequence does not matter, what is left to individualise besides duration and tolerability?

questions.ask: Can an oral receptor degrader improve on the adjuvant endocrine standard?
questions.rationale: Oral degraders outperform an aromatase inhibitor in advanced disease, and the resistance mechanism they were built against is a mutation that emerges under aromatase inhibition. If the mutation is selected by the adjuvant course, a degrader given instead of it, or after it, would remove the pressure that creates the problem.
questions.experiment: Randomisation of a camizestrant or giredestrant course against standard adjuvant endocrine therapy. Two designs are running. One substitutes the degrader upfront in endocrine-naive patients. The other switches into it after two to five years of the standard course.
questions.finding: None has reported.
questions.limitation: The premise is inferred from the advanced setting rather than tested in the adjuvant one. The mutation these drugs were designed for is rare at diagnosis. So the adjuvant question is whether the agent is better against unselected disease, not whether it is better against the mutation. Ten-year endpoints in a subtype whose hazard runs for twenty years will read out on immature data.
questions.next: If an upfront degrader wins, is the gain from the drug or from having removed the aromatase inhibitor that selects the escape?

questions.ask: What is known about the patients the adjuvant endocrine trials did not enrol?
questions.rationale: The adjuvant endocrine record was built almost entirely in postmenopausal women who agreed to take a drug continuously for five years. Two groups sit outside it. Men were excluded from nearly every trial, and women who want to become pregnant were excluded by the design of the intervention.
questions.experiment: For men, a randomised comparison of three endocrine strategies with an endocrine rather than a clinical endpoint. For pregnancy, a single-arm study of a planned treatment interruption, read against an external cohort.
questions.finding: Tamoxifen alone raises circulating oestradiol in men, which is the opposite of its intended effect on the axis, and adding gonadotropin-releasing hormone suppression reverses that. A planned interruption to attempt pregnancy was not followed by an excess of events over the comparison cohort at the follow-up reported.
questions.limitation: Neither design can carry the weight the clinic puts on it. The trial in men measured a hormone rather than a recurrence, so the clinical consequence is inferred. The interruption study had no randomised control and its comparison cohort was assembled separately, and its follow-up is short against a hazard that runs for two decades.
questions.next: Can either group be enrolled in the trials that set the standard, rather than studied separately after the standard has been set?

questions.ask: Which chemotherapy regimen, for the minority of this subtype who need one?
questions.rationale: The adjuvant chemotherapy backbone was built before subtype was used to allocate it. Agents were added one at a time to a regimen that already worked. Each addition was tested in a population enrolled without regard to receptor status. The record a clinic now uses for this subtype was therefore built largely in patients who were not selected to be in it.
questions.experiment: Sequential randomised additions and substitutions on an anthracycline backbone. A taxane added after doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, the interval between cycles shortened with growth factor support, the anthracycline replaced by a taxane and cyclophosphamide, and one taxane and schedule compared against another.
questions.finding: Adding a taxane improved outcomes, shortening the interval improved them, and one four-cycle anthracycline-free regimen matched a taxane and anthracycline combination while a six-cycle version of the same idea did not. Weekly paclitaxel and three-weekly docetaxel each beat three-weekly paclitaxel.
questions.limitation: Almost none of this was randomised within this subtype, and the subtype composition of each trial differs. A regimen comparison that enrolled a mixed population reports an average over subtypes whose sensitivity to chemotherapy is not the same, so a result that holds overall may not hold here. The non-inferiority margins were set separately and are not comparable.
questions.next: Genomic assays now spare most of this subtype chemotherapy altogether. Is the backbone still the right question, or is the question which patients belong in these trials?

questions.ask: What did the cohorts that built the genomic assays actually randomise?
questions.rationale: A genomic assay that allocates chemotherapy has to be validated on material from patients who were randomised to receive it or not. The archival cohorts that made the recurrence score possible were trials run for a different purpose, and their design constrains what the score can be read to establish.
questions.experiment: Retrospective assay of banked tumour from randomised adjuvant trials. Tamoxifen against placebo in node-negative receptor-positive disease, chemotherapy added to tamoxifen in the same population, and chemoendocrine therapy against endocrine therapy alone in node-positive postmenopausal disease.
questions.finding: The score is prognostic in the endocrine-treated arms and predicts chemotherapy benefit in the randomised comparisons, with the benefit concentrated at the high end of the range. The node-positive cohort established that the same relationship holds when nodes are involved.
questions.limitation: These are retrospective analyses of prospectively randomised trials, which is stronger than a cohort and weaker than a trial designed to answer the question. The chemotherapy regimens are decades old and no longer given, so a benefit measured against them may not transfer. The assay was developed on some of the same material it is validated against.
questions.next: Does a score built on the biology of endocrine responsiveness predict benefit from a regimen it never saw?

stories.title: How much chemotherapy a HER2-positive tumour still needs
stories.premise: Most patients in this cell are cured by chemotherapy given with HER2 antibodies. Most of what the cure costs them comes from the chemotherapy rather than from the antibodies. So the questions here are subtractive ones, asked before surgery because that is where the tumour answers back. The specimen grades the response and routes what follows. Every argument in this position turns on how much that grade should be allowed to decide.

chapters.title: Neoadjuvant therapy

questions.ask: Is a pathological complete response worth raising, or is it only a marker of the tumour the patient already had?
questions.rationale: Preoperative and postoperative chemotherapy were compared head to head in operable disease. The order changed nothing about survival. So the reason to treat first is not more cure. It is downstaging of the breast and the axilla. It is also information, because in HER2-positive disease the response is graded on the surgical specimen. That grade separates outcomes steeply.
questions.experiment: The order of the same chemotherapy was randomised in operable disease of every subtype. Within HER2-positive disease, trastuzumab was added to a neoadjuvant anthracycline and taxane backbone in locally advanced and inflammatory tumours, with event-free survival rather than a pathological endpoint as the primary measure. A platform trial with a shared chemotherapy control then followed patients by whether they reached a complete response. Separately, residual invasive disease found at surgery was used as the entry criterion for a trial that randomised what was given afterwards.
questions.finding: The order of treatment does not change survival. What the specimen shows does. Patients who reach a complete response have few events. Those left with residual disease have many. Acting on that residual disease with a conjugate lowers recurrence against continuing the antibody. Adding trastuzumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy raised event-free survival against the same chemotherapy alone, which is the one trial here that measured cure rather than the specimen.
questions.limitation: The association between response and outcome is measured within patients rather than between treatments. A drug that raises the proportion reaching a complete response has not thereby been shown to lower recurrence. The clearest counterexample sits in this cell. The lapatinib and trastuzumab pair raised pathological complete response against trastuzumab before surgery, then failed to improve disease-free survival against trastuzumab when the same combination was tested adjuvantly. The trial that fixed the equivalence of the two orders predates HER2 testing and used chemotherapy nobody now gives. It licenses treating first in general rather than this backbone in particular. The trial that added trastuzumab before surgery enrolled locally advanced and inflammatory disease, which is not the operable population in which the order question was settled.
questions.next: If the endpoint is worth raising at all, what raises it?

questions.ask: Does adding a further drug to trastuzumab and a taxane, or replacing trastuzumab with a better-engineered antibody, raise pathological complete response?
questions.rationale: Trastuzumab binds one epitope. It does not prevent ligand-driven dimerisation. Pertuzumab blocks the dimerisation face. A small-molecule inhibitor blocks the kinase from inside the cell. Engineering the Fc region raises affinity for the activating receptor on immune effector cells. Releasing the brake on T cells asks the same question from the other side, which is whether one antibody leaves HER2 signalling, or immune killing, on the table.
questions.experiment: A second HER2-directed drug was added to trastuzumab on a taxane backbone in separate randomised trials of pertuzumab, of lapatinib and of pyrotinib, each reporting a pathological endpoint. One trial substituted an Fc-engineered antibody for trastuzumab alongside pertuzumab and paclitaxel. One added a checkpoint inhibitor instead of a second HER2-directed drug, with co-primary analyses in all comers and in the PD-L1-positive subset.
questions.finding: Pertuzumab added to trastuzumab and docetaxel raises the proportion reaching a complete response against trastuzumab and docetaxel, in the trial that established the pair and in the trial that repeated it. Pyrotinib added to that same backbone does the same against placebo. Lapatinib is not consistent. Added to trastuzumab on a taxane it raised response against trastuzumab in one trial and fell short of significance in another. The kinase inhibitors buy what they gain with diarrhoea. Improving the antibody rather than adding to it did not raise response against trastuzumab in the same regimen. Nor did adding a checkpoint inhibitor, in either of its co-primary populations.
questions.limitation: The pathological endpoint is not scored the same way across these trials. Some require only the breast to be clear. Others require the nodes as well. The rates therefore cannot be set side by side, even where the regimens nearly match. The backbones differ too, from docetaxel alone, to paclitaxel after an anthracycline, to a dose-dense anthracycline followed by paclitaxel. The trial that repeated the pertuzumab result enrolled an Asian population, which fixes the comparator rather than widening it. The third lapatinib trial, the one that gave a taxane with no anthracycline, has published long-term survival and gene expression rather than the pathological comparison it was designed around. It cannot be counted on either side of the lapatinib question. The Fc-engineering result exists only as conference and registry material, with no primary publication. Its unsuccessful comparison cannot be read at the level of detail the others allow.
questions.next: If the antibodies are doing this much of the work, how much of the chemotherapy beside them is still earning its place?

questions.ask: Can the anthracycline come out of the neoadjuvant backbone, and what should stand in its place?
questions.rationale: An anthracycline costs cardiac function and carries a small leukaemia risk. It is given alongside an antibody that itself depresses left ventricular function. The pivotal adjuvant trial that ran a trastuzumab regimen with and without an anthracycline had already found the two close. That made the omission worth testing where the readout is fast.
questions.experiment: A cardiac safety trial ran three dual-blockade regimens before surgery, one of them carrying no anthracycline, with the pathological endpoint secondary. A randomised trial then varied the anthracycline alone, on a fixed taxane, carboplatin and dual-blockade backbone, with response as the endpoint and event-free survival on follow-up. Separately, carboplatin was added to a taxane and anthracycline backbone in a trial enrolling both triple-negative and HER2-positive disease. A further trial set weekly nab-paclitaxel with dual blockade against docetaxel and carboplatin with dual blockade, neither arm carrying an anthracycline. The taxane formulation was isolated on its own in an all-comers trial where both arms kept the anthracycline.
questions.finding: Dropping the anthracycline did not cost event-free survival against keeping it, on a backbone that was otherwise identical. In the cardiac safety trial the anthracycline-free regimen produced responses in the same range as the two regimens containing one. Symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction appeared there only in the arms that carried an anthracycline. Adding platinum raised response in triple-negative disease and added nothing in the HER2-positive stratum of the same trial, with a formal test of interaction separating the two. Among anthracycline-free regimens, weekly nab-paclitaxel with dual blockade raised response against docetaxel and carboplatin with dual blockade. Substituting nab-paclitaxel for solvent-based paclitaxel also raised response in the all-comers trial that changed nothing else.
questions.limitation: The trial that varied the anthracycline alone was sized on the pathological endpoint. Its event-free survival comparison is a follow-up analysis on few events. The absence of a difference there is not a demonstration of equivalence. The cardiac safety trial put response second and never compared its arms formally, so its three rates sit beside each other rather than against each other. The comparison that favoured nab-paclitaxel in HER2-positive disease changed two things at once, the taxane formulation and the carboplatin. It cannot say which change produced the gain. It also enrolled Asian patients only. The trial that isolates the formulation kept the anthracycline in both arms and enrolled every subtype, so it settles that question outside this cell rather than inside it. The platinum question was answered in a stratum of a trial powered for the triple-negative population.
questions.next: If the anthracycline is dispensable, is the rest of the cytotoxic backbone dispensable too?

questions.ask: Can conventional chemotherapy be left out altogether and the HER2 block given alone?
questions.rationale: Some HER2-positive tumours depend on the receptor to the point of addiction. In the trial that established the antibody pair, the arm given both antibodies without a taxane still produced complete responses in a minority of patients. If those tumours can be identified, the cytotoxic drug is being given to them for nothing.
questions.experiment: Chemotherapy-free dual blockade was given for a fixed window before surgery, with endocrine therapy added for oestrogen receptor-positive disease, across a series of single-arm and randomised phase II trials. One randomised the length of that window, a shorter course against a longer one. One asked whether the intrinsic subtype called from the diagnostic biopsy predicts who responds. One tested formally whether early responders given dual blockade alone could be spared the taxane.
questions.finding: Chemotherapy-free blockade produces complete responses in a minority. That minority is larger with the longer window than with the shorter one. It is larger in oestrogen receptor-negative than in receptor-positive disease. It is larger in tumours called HER2-enriched than in the rest. The trial that tested omission formally did not show non-inferiority against the taxane. On that test the taxane was not dispensable, even in early responders.
questions.limitation: Most of these trials have no chemotherapy arm and no survival endpoint. Nothing in them can support equivalence to chemotherapy. The duration trial combined a phase II design in its experimental arm with a pick-the-winner design and was explicitly not powered to compare the two windows. The gap between them is a numerical difference that was never tested. The trial that did test omission set early responders in the chemotherapy-free arm against every patient in the taxane arm, which compares a selected group with an unselected one. It also enrolled hormone receptor-negative disease only. The subtype trial had no comparator. A subtype that identifies responders to chemotherapy-free blockade has not thereby been shown to identify patients who can forgo chemotherapy. The single-arm windows and the duration trial all used lapatinib with trastuzumab rather than the antibody pair now given, so their rates do not transfer to the regimen a clinic would actually use.
questions.next: If blanket omission fails, can the patients who can safely omit be picked out instead, either before treatment or from their response to it?

questions.ask: Can the response to the first weeks of treatment decide who needs chemotherapy, rather than the decision being made for everyone in advance?
questions.rationale: A baseline assay predicts. A short exposure tests. A tumour whose metabolic activity collapses under antibody alone has demonstrated the dependence an assay was trying to infer. The same logic applies at the other end of the course, because a complete response at surgery is the strongest evidence a tumour can give that what it received was enough.
questions.experiment: One trial randomised a response-adapted strategy against chemotherapy with dual blockade, giving antibodies alone and adding chemotherapy only to patients whose tumours failed to respond on imaging. One tested formally whether the metabolic change measured early in the first cycle predicts pathological complete response, against a prespecified accuracy threshold. Others adapted at the far end, using magnetic resonance imaging to decide when enough chemotherapy had been given, or withholding further chemotherapy from patients whose specimen showed a complete response.
questions.finding: Imaging separates responders from non-responders early. The adapted groups have done well on the endpoints reported so far. Adherence to withholding chemotherapy after a complete response was high where it was measured against a feasibility target. The formal test of predictive accuracy missed its prespecified threshold. The signal underneath it was real, since tumours without a substantial metabolic fall rarely reached a complete response.
questions.limitation: The randomised response-adapted trial reported its recurrence endpoint against a fixed threshold rather than against its own comparator arm. That arm was small by design. So the strategy was measured against an expectation rather than against chemotherapy. The trials that adapt on the pathological response are single-arm. Their recurrence and survival endpoints have since been reported and are excellent, and that changes nothing about the inference. With no comparator, an excellent outcome after a complete response describes the prognosis of a responder rather than the effect of stopping. The trial that tested metabolic prediction required oestrogen receptor-negative disease. It says nothing about the receptor-positive majority, where complete responses are least common and the decision is hardest.
questions.next: If what is being avoided is systemic cytotoxic exposure, can the cytotoxic be carried to the target instead of given free?

questions.ask: Can an antibody-drug conjugate replace conventional chemotherapy before surgery?
questions.rationale: A conjugate delivers a cytotoxic to cells that display the target. In a tumour selected for displaying that target, it ought to reproduce the cell kill of chemotherapy while sparing everything else much of the exposure. The neoadjuvant setting reads that claim out in months rather than years.
questions.experiment: The substitution was made randomly before surgery, conjugate with pertuzumab against docetaxel, carboplatin and dual blockade, with pathological complete response as the endpoint. In hormone receptor-positive disease the same conjugate was randomised against trastuzumab with endocrine therapy. The substitution was also tested after surgery, conjugate with pertuzumab against a taxane with dual blockade, both arms following an anthracycline. A single-arm study of conjugate with pertuzumab defined heterogeneous and non-heterogeneous tumours prospectively, from biopsies taken at more than one site in each tumour rather than from a single score. A newer conjugate was then tested not as a replacement for chemotherapy but as the opening of the regimen, against an anthracycline opening, with the same antibody and taxane triplet completing both.
questions.finding: Substituting the conjugate for chemotherapy before surgery lowered response against that chemotherapy, even though severe adverse events were far less frequent than on the chemotherapy it replaced. The same substitution after surgery did not improve freedom from invasive disease against the taxane with dual blockade. The heterogeneity study accounts for part of the shortfall, because tumours carrying regions without the target essentially did not respond, while tumours uniform for it responded well. The newer conjugate, placed before the taxane triplet rather than instead of it, raised response against the anthracycline opening.
questions.limitation: The heterogeneity comparison was planned prospectively. Its groups were still not randomised. Only a small minority of evaluable tumours were heterogeneous, so the response rate in that group rests on very few patients. The hormone receptor-positive conjugate trial used trastuzumab with endocrine therapy as its control, a comparator with no cytotoxic content at all. Beating it says nothing about replacing chemotherapy. The adjuvant comparison is a different question in a different setting, since both of its arms also received an anthracycline. The newer conjugate was tested in high-risk disease only. Its event-free survival is barely mature. Its winning arm still contains a taxane. These are different questions about conjugates rather than repeated confirmations of one.
questions.next: If a target-positive report can conceal regions without the target, should HER2 be recorded as a proportion of the tumour rather than as a score on one block, and would routing on that proportion change who is offered a conjugate?

stories.title: Matching adjuvant HER2 treatment to baseline risk
stories.premise: Before the antibody, HER2 amplification carried the worst prognosis in early breast cancer. It now carries one of the best, on a regimen whose chemotherapy backbone, whose duration and whose stopping point were all fixed in trials built on node-positive and high-risk disease. Most patients treated with it today sit well below that risk, so the questions here run along one axis in both directions at once: what can be taken away at the bottom, and what has to be added at the top.

chapters.title: Deciding whether to treat before surgery
Adjuvant and post-neoadjuvant therapy

questions.ask: Does adding a year of trastuzumab to adjuvant chemotherapy lower recurrence?
questions.rationale: HER2 amplification marked the fastest-relapsing early breast cancer of the pre-antibody era. The antibody already worked against established metastatic disease. Micrometastatic disease left behind after surgery should be the easier target, being smaller and less heterogeneous than a measurable metastasis.
questions.experiment: Adjuvant programmes randomised trastuzumab against no trastuzumab on a chemotherapy backbone. They differ in whether the antibody ran concurrently with the taxane or began only after all chemotherapy. They differ again in whether the backbone contained an anthracycline, and in how long the antibody was continued.
questions.finding: Recurrence fell in every comparison. The separation was still open at the longest follow-up any of them reported. The anthracycline-free backbone gave disease control close to that of the anthracycline backbone, with less cardiac dysfunction.
questions.limitation: A year of antibody was a protocol convention rather than a tested dose, so these trials establish that the antibody works without establishing how much of it is needed. The trial that compared the antibody against observation allowed its control group to cross over once the first results were public, so its long-term survival comparison is diluted by design. The two trastuzumab backbones in the anthracycline comparison were never set against each other under a non-inferiority design. The absence of a significant difference between them is therefore an absence of evidence and not a demonstration of equivalence. The short-course signal that prompted everything downstream came from a small HER2-positive substudy nested inside a randomisation of two different chemotherapies.
questions.next: If a year was chosen rather than found, can less than a year hold the same disease control?

questions.ask: Can adjuvant trastuzumab be shortened below a year without losing disease control?
questions.rationale: The year was inherited from the pivotal protocols rather than derived from them. It carries cardiac risk, a long course of infusions, and a cost that decides access in much of the world. The nested short course suggested the antibody might do most of its work early.
questions.experiment: Two trials randomised six months of the antibody against the standard year. Two more randomised a nine-week course against it. Each set its own non-inferiority margin, and not all on the same scale. The pivotal observation trial had already tested the question from the other end by randomising a second year against the first.
questions.finding: A second year bought nothing over the first. Of the shortened comparisons, only one was declared non-inferior. Both nine-week comparisons pointed against the short course, one of them with a point estimate a long way from equivalence. Cardiac events were fewer on the shorter arms wherever they were counted.
questions.limitation: These results do not stack. Estimates that look alike did not answer alike. The two six-month trials returned closely similar hazard ratios and reached opposite verdicts. One set its margin as a difference in percentage points of disease-free survival at a fixed time point, and the other set its margin on the hazard ratio scale, so the verdict turns on the scale as much as on the estimate. The chemotherapy partners differ across these trials, as does the point at which the antibody started relative to them. None randomised duration inside a defined risk stratum, so failing non-inferiority in an unselected population says nothing about whether a small node-negative tumour needs the full year.
questions.next: If the duration cannot be cut for everyone, can the chemotherapy be cut for the patients whose baseline risk is lowest?

questions.ask: For a small node-negative HER2-positive tumour, how little chemotherapy is enough?
questions.rationale: The pivotal trials were built on node-positive and high-risk disease and prescribed an anthracycline followed by a taxane. Small node-negative tumours were largely excluded from them. Those tumours still recur, so they are still treated. They are asked to carry a toxicity that was justified against a much higher baseline risk.
questions.experiment: One trial gave a single-group adjuvant course of a weekly taxane with trastuzumab in node-negative disease below a size cut-off. A second randomised the antibody-drug conjugate against that same taxane-and-antibody pair, with a protocol-defined composite of clinically relevant toxicity as a co-primary endpoint alongside invasive disease-free survival. From the neoadjuvant side, a third tested whether patients responding early to dual blockade could be spared the taxane altogether.
questions.finding: Almost everyone given the short taxane-and-antibody course was free of invasive disease at the primary analysis, and the great majority still were at the long-term report. The conjugate arm reached a very low rate of invasive disease of its own. It did not lower the composite toxicity endpoint, which was the comparison that trial was built to make. Dropping the taxane from dual blockade lost pathological response, including among the early responders it was designed to protect.
questions.limitation: The single-group trial has no control arm, so its outcome measures the population selected into it as much as the regimen given to it. The substitution trial was powered for toxicity rather than for a disease-free survival comparison, and it allocated most of its patients to the conjugate while keeping only a small taxane comparator. Its outcome arms therefore cannot establish equivalence. Its null toxicity result is also a statement about a composite. The totals matched, which is not the same as the two regimens costing a patient the same things. The taxane-omission question was settled on pathological response rather than on recurrence, in hormone receptor-negative disease only, with very few patients in each response group.
questions.next: If the floor can be lowered this far for low-risk disease, does the ceiling need raising for node-positive disease?

questions.ask: Does escalating beyond chemotherapy and a year of trastuzumab lower recurrence, and if so for whom?
questions.rationale: A second antibody binds a different epitope and blocks the dimerisation that trastuzumab leaves intact. Neoadjuvant trials had already shown that the pair raises pathological complete response above the single antibody. A kinase inhibitor offers the same second block from inside the cell, and a conjugate offers to carry the cytotoxic to the target rather than through the patient. The adjuvant question is whether any of that converts into fewer recurrences years later.
questions.experiment: One trial randomised pertuzumab against placebo on top of chemotherapy and a year of trastuzumab, in node-positive and high-risk node-negative disease. A second tested a different route to a dual block, randomising a kinase inhibitor given with trastuzumab, or sequenced after it, against trastuzumab alone. A third kept pertuzumab running through both arms and replaced the taxane and trastuzumab portion of the regimen with the conjugate.
questions.finding: The second antibody lowered invasive recurrence, with the gain sitting in the node-positive stratum and nothing to show in node-negative disease. The kinase inhibitor given concurrently fell short of its significance threshold. Sequencing it after trastuzumab added nothing at all. The conjugate substitution did not improve on the taxane arm on either of its co-primary populations.
questions.limitation: The nodal split is a subgroup gradient inside one randomisation rather than a randomised comparison of two populations. Overall survival in that trial has not separated. The kinase inhibitor's concurrent arm was judged against a threshold tightened after a third arm closed for futility, so the same estimate reads as a narrow miss or as a small real benefit depending on which threshold is applied to it. The conjugate's null result is a failure to improve on an active control and not evidence of an inactive drug. Far fewer patients completed treatment on the conjugate arm, so it compares strategies as delivered rather than drugs as prescribed.
questions.next: If a second antibody pays only at higher nodal risk, does a drug with a different mechanism help the patients still at risk once the year of blockade has finished?

questions.ask: Does extending HER2-directed treatment beyond the first year add anything?
questions.rationale: Recurrences keep arriving after the antibody stops, and in hormone receptor-positive disease they arrive late. Whether more time on treatment helps at all had already been put to the antibody itself. An irreversible pan-HER kinase inhibitor acts inside the cell and covers signalling the antibody leaves intact, including the crosstalk with the oestrogen receptor that is one proposed route of escape.
questions.experiment: The pivotal observation trial had randomised a second year of the antibody against one. The extension trial randomised a further year of the kinase inhibitor against placebo in patients who had completed trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy, stratified by hormone receptor status, with invasive disease-free survival read at a fixed early landmark as the primary endpoint.
questions.finding: A second year of the antibody itself added nothing over the first. The kinase inhibitor lowered invasive recurrence inside that early window. Severe diarrhoea was far more common than on placebo. By the final analysis the two arms had the same overall survival.
questions.limitation: An early landmark is a short window for the very group the drug is now aimed at, whose recurrences come late, so the primary result was read before the population it selects for had time to relapse. Hormone receptor status was a stratification factor and not a randomised comparison of the strata. The trial enrolled before adjuvant pertuzumab and before conjugate treatment for residual disease, so almost nobody in it had received the treatment a candidate would receive today. No antidiarrhoeal strategy was part of the randomisation, so the tolerability on record is the tolerability of the drug given without one.
questions.next: Every escalation and every de-escalation here is allocated on nodal status and tumour size measured before a drop of treatment is given. Can the tumour's own response to treatment allocate it better?

questions.ask: What decides whether a HER2-positive tumour goes to treatment first or to surgery first?
questions.rationale: Every other question in this part assumes the setting has already been chosen. The choice itself is the first decision a clinic takes, and it determines what can be learned and what can be offered afterwards. Treating first makes the response measurable and opens post-neoadjuvant escalation. Operating first closes both and allows a lighter regimen.
questions.experiment: No trial randomises the order. What exists instead are two separate bodies of evidence built in populations defined by the choice. Single-group and randomised de-escalation studies in small node-negative tumours taken to surgery first, and randomised escalation on residual disease in tumours treated first.
questions.finding: Both strategies work in the populations they were tested in. A small node-negative tumour does well on a markedly reduced adjuvant regimen. A tumour with residual disease after preoperative treatment does better when treatment is escalated on that finding.
questions.limitation: The comparison a clinic wants has never been randomised, and the two bodies of evidence enrolled different disease. Reading them together makes the choice look settled at the extremes and leaves it unevidenced in the middle, which is where most patients are. The eligibility criteria, not the results, are what separate the two literatures.
questions.next: If preoperative treatment is what makes escalation possible, is a tumour small enough for de-escalation also small enough that nothing would have been found to escalate on?

stories.title: Escalating treatment on residual disease after HER2 blockade
stories.premise: Residual invasive disease at surgery is the strongest selection rule in early breast cancer, because it is measured rather than inferred. The tumour met HER2-directed therapy and was still there at operation. Every question in this position therefore concerns a population defined by a failure that has already happened, and by how much of that population each trial agreed to enrol.

chapters.title: Adjuvant and post-neoadjuvant therapy

questions.ask: For residual invasive disease at surgery, does switching to an antibody-drug conjugate lower recurrence more than completing the planned trastuzumab?
questions.rationale: Residual disease is observed resistance rather than inferred risk. The tumour met trastuzumab and a taxane and was still present at operation. Completing the same antibody asks a drug to finish work it has already been shown not to do in that patient. A conjugate keeps the target and changes the mechanism, by delivering a cytotoxic to a cell the antibody can still find. The selection rule itself was not new when it reached this subtype. Escalating chemotherapy on residual disease had already lowered recurrence in HER2-negative disease.
questions.experiment: KATHERINE randomised patients with residual invasive disease in the breast or axilla after neoadjuvant taxane-based chemotherapy with trastuzumab to trastuzumab emtansine or to completing trastuzumab, with invasive disease-free survival as the primary endpoint. CREATE-X had tested the same selection rule in HER2-negative residual disease, with capecitabine as the escalation. Beside both sits KAITLIN, which gave the same conjugate with pertuzumab after upfront surgery in place of the taxane. Its patients were selected by nodal status and tumour size rather than by residual disease. It is the same drug asked to work without the selection rule.
questions.finding: In selected residual disease the conjugate lowered invasive recurrence against continuing the antibody. Follow-up ran long enough for that recurrence benefit to become an overall survival benefit, which is uncommon in this setting. The selection rule had already held outside the subtype, where post-neoadjuvant capecitabine lowered recurrence and lengthened survival in HER2-negative residual disease. Where the rule was absent the conjugate did nothing. In the adjuvant population it matched the taxane with dual antibody on invasive disease-free survival. Fewer patients completed the planned course.
questions.limitation: The control arm was the drug the tumour had already grown through. What the trial establishes is that a conjugate beats continuing an agent known to have failed in that patient. It does not establish that the conjugate beats any other escalation that might have been offered. The entry rule was also loose about what the tumour had been exposed to. An anthracycline was optional. Most patients were treated before pertuzumab was routine. Residual disease in the trial therefore followed a weaker regimen than residual disease in clinic today. The capecitabine trial supplies the principle but not the subtype, because it enrolled HER2-negative disease only.
questions.next: If the class is right, does a conjugate with a different payload beat the one that established the setting?

questions.ask: Does a bystander-capable conjugate lower recurrence further than the conjugate that established this setting?
questions.rationale: The first conjugate carries a payload that stays inside the cell it enters. It therefore kills only cells that bind and internalise enough antibody. Residual disease after HER2 blockade is the compartment most likely to carry reduced or patchy antigen. A cleavable payload that crosses into neighbouring cells should reach what the first conjugate cannot. A single-arm neoadjuvant study had already reported no responses at all to the non-bystander conjugate where HER2 was spatially heterogeneous.
questions.experiment: DESTINY-Breast05 randomised trastuzumab deruxtecan against trastuzumab emtansine in residual invasive disease, with entry restricted to node-positive disease at surgery or inoperable disease at diagnosis. The comparator was the established conjugate rather than the antibody. This is the first trial in this position whose control arm was already known to work. The antigen argument behind it comes from the heterogeneity study, which gave the older conjugate with pertuzumab before surgery and compared prospectively defined heterogeneous and non-heterogeneous tumours.
questions.finding: The newer conjugate lowered invasive recurrence against an active comparator. Drug-related interstitial lung disease was far more frequent than on the older conjugate. Patients on the newer conjugate died of it. In the heterogeneity study no tumour with spatially heterogeneous HER2 reached a pathological complete response, against a substantial response rate in the tumours called homogeneous.
questions.limitation: Recurrence was the endpoint that reported. Overall survival was immature at the primary analysis. A pulmonary toxicity that killed patients is therefore being weighed against a recurrence endpoint whose survival counterpart has not yet read out. The enrolled population was also narrower than that of the trial it displaced, because residual disease with negative nodes at surgery was not admitted. The antigen reasoning rests on a single-arm study whose heterogeneous and non-heterogeneous groups were prospectively defined but never randomised, with very few heterogeneous tumours among them. Heterogeneity there was read off two biopsies per tumour against a fixed cut-off for the proportion of amplified cells. The exposure variable there is a sampling scheme and a scoring convention before it is a property of the disease.
questions.next: Does the benefit reach the residual-disease patients the trial did not enrol?

questions.ask: Does low-volume residual disease with negative nodes at surgery need the same escalation as residual nodal disease?
questions.rationale: Residual disease is a category rather than a quantity. A small deposit left in the breast with clear nodes carries a different hazard from disease still in the nodes after treatment. Trials have written that gradient into their entry criteria instead of testing it, which converts a biological question into an eligibility question.
questions.experiment: Read the entry criteria against each other rather than the results. KATHERINE admitted any residual invasive disease in the breast or axilla. DESTINY-Breast05 required node-positive disease at surgery or inoperable disease at diagnosis. The two randomised additions still running narrow entry further. CompassHER2 RD admits oestrogen receptor-negative or node-positive residual disease. ASTEFANIA admits residual disease called high-risk.
questions.finding: The randomised record is dense where risk is highest and thin where it is lowest. For residual disease with negative nodes, the only randomised evidence is still the older comparison against the antibody. The newer conjugate is untested in exactly the group whose absolute risk is smallest.
questions.limitation: Nodal status after neoadjuvant therapy is a staging convention as much as a biological variable. It depends on how the axilla was sampled and on how many nodes were examined. A patient called node-negative after a sentinel procedure has not had the same test as one after a dissection. No trial randomised the threshold itself. The line between escalating and not escalating is an eligibility rule that was chosen once and then inherited by the trials that followed.
questions.next: For a patient outside the newer trial's entry criteria, is there anything worth adding to the established conjugate instead?

questions.ask: Does adding a second agent to the established post-neoadjuvant conjugate lower recurrence further?
questions.rationale: Once systemic control improves in this subtype, a large share of first relapses arrive in the brain. A conjugate is a poor drug for that site. The obvious partner is therefore the small molecule that has intracranial activity in metastatic disease. Residual disease has also survived in an intact immune context, which is the separate argument for adding a checkpoint antibody.
questions.experiment: Two randomised trials add an agent to the established conjugate in residual disease. CompassHER2 RD adds tucatinib against placebo, with entry restricted to oestrogen receptor-negative or node-positive disease. ASTEFANIA adds atezolizumab against placebo in high-risk residual disease. The case for each partner was made elsewhere. HER2CLIMB tested tucatinib in metastatic disease already treated with the antibodies and the conjugate. It enrolled patients with brain metastases. IMpassion050 tested a checkpoint antibody added to preoperative chemotherapy and dual blockade.
questions.finding: Neither addition has reported. The only publication on the record for the immunotherapy trial is its design protocol. The enrolment figure attached to that record is a plan rather than a count of patients randomised. The borrowed evidence points in two directions. Tucatinib lengthened progression-free and overall survival in previously treated metastatic disease. It also delayed progression in the patients with brain metastases. The checkpoint antibody did not raise pathological complete response before surgery in this subtype. It did not do so in the tumours selected for PD-L1 expression either.
questions.limitation: Both trials were designed when the established conjugate was the only post-neoadjuvant option. A positive result will therefore show that an addition improves on a backbone that a newer conjugate has already beaten in node-positive residual disease. No trial compares those two strategies against each other. The tucatinib evidence also comes from disease that had already progressed on the conjugate in the metastatic setting, which is not the same biology as disease left behind at surgery. The checkpoint evidence comes from before surgery and reports a response endpoint. It constrains the immunotherapy question without settling it.
questions.next: When the conjugate course is finished and the risk is not, is there anything to give next?

questions.ask: After the post-neoadjuvant conjugate is completed, is there anything more to offer a patient whose risk continues?
questions.rationale: Recurrence in this population goes on after the planned cycles of conjugate end. The escalation therefore stops while the hazard is still running. Extended oral pan-HER inhibition after the antibody is finished is the only continuation that has been randomised in this subtype.
questions.experiment: ExteNET randomised extended neratinib against placebo after completion of trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy, with randomisation stratified by hormone receptor status. The population was defined by having finished trastuzumab rather than by residual disease. Patients with residual disease sit inside the trial as a fraction of it.
questions.finding: Extension lowered invasive recurrence against placebo over the early years of follow-up. The effect was concentrated in hormone receptor-positive disease. Long-term overall survival was no different between the arms. Severe diarrhoea was common.
questions.limitation: The trial predates routine pertuzumab. It predates post-neoadjuvant conjugates entirely. Nobody in it had received the treatment that now defines this position. The diarrhoea on record was collected without mandatory antidiarrhoeal prophylaxis, which is a statement about how the trial was run rather than about the drug as it is given now. The hormone receptor restriction that governs current use is a comparison between two randomisation strata rather than a randomised comparison, however well balanced those strata were. Eligibility was also narrowed partway through accrual. The population enrolled is not the one the protocol opened with.
questions.next: If everything available after surgery is constrained by what was given before it, does a better preoperative regimen dissolve this question or only move it?

questions.ask: Does a stronger preoperative regimen remove the population this whole strategy was built for?
questions.rationale: Every question in this position presupposes residual disease at surgery. The preoperative regimen decides how many patients arrive with it and which ones they are. It also decides which drugs remain unused, because a conjugate spent before surgery is not available after it.
questions.experiment: Three trials move that boundary in different directions. DESTINY-Breast11 randomised a conjugate given alone, or followed by the taxane with dual antibody, against dose-dense anthracycline chemotherapy followed by the same triplet. CompassHER2 pCR gave a chemotherapy-light preoperative regimen in a single arm and omitted further chemotherapy after a pathological complete response. KRISTINE substituted the older conjugate with pertuzumab for chemotherapy altogether.
questions.finding: The conjugate sequence raised pathological complete response against the anthracycline standard, which shrinks the residual-disease population. The chemotherapy-light regimen left most patients with residual disease. Those patients were predominantly oestrogen receptor-positive. Substituting the conjugate for chemotherapy lowered pathological complete response and enlarged the residual-disease population. Acute toxicity on that arm was much lower. Recurrence on follow-up was nonetheless more frequent than on chemotherapy. The substitution cost more than it saved.
questions.limitation: All three moved a surrogate first. Pathological complete response is the endpoint that reports early. Event-free survival in DESTINY-Breast11 was immature at the primary report. Enrolment in its conjugate-alone arm also closed early. What survives from it is a comparison of two sequences rather than of a conjugate against chemotherapy. The response-adapted trial has not reported its recurrence endpoint at all. Nothing has randomised what to do about residual disease that persisted through a preoperative conjugate. Every post-neoadjuvant trial in this position enrolled tumours that survived an antibody and a taxane. A tumour that survives trastuzumab deruxtecan before surgery is a different population with no evidence behind it.
questions.next: Should the escalation rule be written in terms of what the tumour was exposed to rather than what is left in the specimen?

stories.title: Taking the chemotherapy out when the oestrogen receptor is also on
stories.premise: Triple-positive disease is treated by two traditions and belongs to neither. It clears less completely under a taxane with HER2 blockade than receptor-negative HER2-positive disease does. It also keeps a second driver that endocrine therapy can reach. So the neoadjuvant argument here is about what that second driver lets a clinic take away, and about how anyone would know in advance which patient it is safe to take it from.

chapters.title: Early triple-positive disease

questions.ask: Why does pathological complete response fall when the oestrogen receptor is also expressed?
questions.rationale: The two receptors talk to each other. Blocking HER2 lifts the suppression it exerts on oestrogen receptor signalling. A tumour carrying both can therefore shift its dependence instead of dying. A tumour with somewhere to go should be harder to eradicate before surgery than one without.
questions.experiment: The neoadjuvant HER2 trials stratified randomisation by hormone receptor status and reported response within each stratum. Between them they cover a taxane with one antibody, a taxane with an antibody and a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, a taxane with two antibodies, and a conjugate substituted for the taxane. The same split was reported in the large modern single-arm cohort given a taxane with dual blockade. Separately, intrinsic subtype was called on pretreatment biopsies in chemotherapy-free cohorts and set against response, in one cohort that admitted any receptor status and in one restricted to receptor-positive disease.
questions.finding: Wherever the split is reported, response is lower in the receptor-positive stratum than in the receptor-negative one. Intensifying the HER2 blockade raises response in both strata without closing the distance between them. Substituting a conjugate for the taxane does not close it either. What separates the receptor-positive tumours that clear from the rest is whether the pretreatment biopsy is called HER2-enriched.
questions.limitation: Hormone receptor status was a stratification factor and a reporting subgroup in these trials. It was never randomised. The two strata therefore differ in more than the receptor. The endpoint is not the same endpoint across them either. Some scored the breast alone and some the breast and the axilla. Receptor-positive tumours are also where low-volume residual disease concentrates, so where the line between a complete response and a near-complete one is drawn changes the size of the gap it produces. Subtype was called by a signature assay run on a single pretreatment core, which classifies that core rather than the tumour.
questions.next: If the oestrogen receptor is the escape route, does blocking it and the cell cycle it feeds, at the same time as HER2, close the route?

questions.ask: Does blocking the oestrogen receptor, HER2 and the cell cycle at once let the taxane be left out?
questions.rationale: Both receptors converge on cyclin D and CDK4/6. That node is where a tumour switching drivers has to pass. Blocking it as well as both receptors should close the escape route rather than leave it open. It should do so with no cytotoxic anywhere in the regimen.
questions.experiment: A single-arm study gave dual HER2 antibodies with a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a receptor degrader before surgery. Its coprimary readouts were the change in proliferation at two weeks and again at surgery, and the change in apoptosis by surgery. Response was only a secondary endpoint there. A randomised phase II trial then substituted a CDK4/6 inhibitor with an aromatase inhibitor for weekly paclitaxel, keeping the same two antibodies in both arms.
