Its primary question was neither of the two response rates. It asked whether a gene signature of E2F pathway activity predicted which arm a tumour would do better on.
questions.finding: Proliferation collapses within two weeks of starting the chemotherapy-free triplet. It has risen again by surgery without returning to baseline. Apoptosis fell over the same interval rather than rising, which is the opposite direction to the one the design expected. When the substitution was put against a taxane, the trial's own primary question came back negative. The signature did not identify an arm for a tumour to prefer. The two arms reached the same response rate, which is a descriptive comparison and not the thing the trial was built to test.
questions.limitation: The single-arm study had no control group. Its primary endpoint was the change in proliferation rather than response, so what it shows is that the drugs are reaching their target and not that the strategy suffices. Its first cohort was small, and several of the patients in it turned out on retrospective review not to be HER2-positive. The randomised trial was not designed as a non-inferiority comparison, so two response estimates that land in the same place are not evidence that the chemotherapy-free arm is as good as the taxane. Its population was postmenopausal and at the older end of the range, which is narrower than the group the strategy would be offered to. Its signature was read by sequencing a pretreatment biopsy, so a null interaction is a verdict on that assay as much as on the biology behind it.
questions.next: If adding cell-cycle blockade can match a taxane without being shown to replace it, how much can be taken away with HER2 blockade and endocrine therapy alone?

questions.ask: Can HER2 blockade with endocrine therapy and no cytotoxic clear enough disease to leave the taxane out?
questions.rationale: Dual HER2 blockade eradicates a real fraction of tumours by itself. In receptor-positive disease endocrine therapy is on hand to hold the other pathway while it does. If the pair is enough for a substantial minority, then the taxane is being given to everyone in order to reach the rest.
questions.experiment: The trial that established neoadjuvant dual blockade carried an arm of the two antibodies with no chemotherapy at all. Dedicated studies followed. One was a single-arm window of an antibody with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor and concurrent oestrogen deprivation. A second randomised that same window for duration. A third gave a conjugate with or without endocrine therapy and set both against a bare antibody with endocrine therapy. Two trials then put a chemotherapy-free arm against a cytotoxic one, substituting a conjugate for docetaxel and carboplatin in the first and endocrine therapy for weekly paclitaxel in the second.
questions.finding: A chemotherapy-free window clears disease in a minority of receptor-positive tumours. It leaves low-volume residual disease in many more of them, and that residue concentrates in the receptor-positive group rather than the receptor-negative one. Longer exposure produced more complete responses than shorter exposure in the one trial that randomised duration. That gain sat in the receptor-positive subgroup. Adding endocrine therapy to a conjugate changed response not at all, while dropping the conjugate for a bare antibody with the same endocrine therapy cut response to a fraction of it. Against a cytotoxic comparator the chemotherapy-free arms lose response, by a little when a conjugate carries the payload and by a lot when nothing cytotoxic is given at all. The conjugate arm also carried the higher risk of an event-free survival event on longer follow-up. Severe adverse events were far less frequent without the cytotoxic in the trial that reported them.
questions.limitation: The duration trial combined a phase II design in its experimental arm with a pick-the-winner design and was not powered to compare the two durations, so its gap is a numerical difference with no test behind it. Its duration effect also sat in the receptor-positive subgroup of a trial that admitted any receptor status, which is a subgroup of a design that was not asking about receptors. Both windows used an antibody with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, which is not the dual blockade a clinic gives today. The conjugate comparison and the endocrine comparison were both sized for response, so their survival curves are secondary readouts on samples chosen for a different endpoint. The interval around the endocrine trial's survival estimate is wide enough to hold very different truths.
questions.next: If a chemotherapy-free regimen clears disease in some patients and not in others, can the ones it will clear be picked out before treatment starts, or early enough to change it?

questions.ask: Can the patients who can safely be spared chemotherapy be identified in advance, or from their early response?
questions.rationale: A chemotherapy-free strategy is only defensible if it is offered to tumours that will answer it. Two kinds of marker were proposed for that. One is read on the pretreatment biopsy and says what the tumour is. The other is read after a short exposure and says what the tumour does.
questions.experiment: On the baseline side, intrinsic subtype was called on pretreatment biopsies in two chemotherapy-free cohorts. HER2 was scored prospectively on biopsies taken from two separate sites of each tumour before a conjugate given with a second antibody and no chemotherapy. A signature of E2F pathway activity was tested as a formal treatment interaction in the randomised substitution trial. On the dynamic side, a fall in proliferation after two weeks of an aromatase inhibitor was used to route patients either to a chemotherapy-free regimen or to a taxane. Metabolic response on imaging was used the same way, with chemotherapy added only on failure to respond. Pathological response at surgery was used to assign what came after it, in a single-arm strategy trial and in a large response-adapted cohort.
questions.finding: Baseline biology separates the population. Tumours called HER2-enriched respond far more often than tumours that are not, both in a cohort of any receptor status and within the receptor-positive route of the trial that allocated on proliferation. Tumours whose HER2 scores as heterogeneous across the same specimen did not respond at all to a conjugate given without chemotherapy. The one marker tested as a treatment interaction rather than as a prognostic split, the E2F signature, showed no interaction with the treatment given. Early response separates the population too, although the route it sent molecular responders down cleared only a minority of them. The imaging-guided pathway that withholds chemotherapy from responders holds up on freedom from invasive disease against the threshold it was set.
questions.limitation: The subtype and heterogeneity results come from cohorts that were not randomised on the marker, so they say who responds and not who needed the chemotherapy that was withheld. Heterogeneity in particular is a sampling convention rather than a property of the disease. It is two biopsies from one tumour scored against a threshold, and only a small handful of tumours met that definition, so the contrast rests on a very small denominator. In the trial that routed on proliferation the two routes were given different treatments, so the higher response among the non-responders is the paclitaxel they were sent to and not a failure of the marker. The response-adapted trials measure their strategy against a fixed expectation rather than against the same patients treated the other way, and a patient who has declared herself a responder is by construction one who was going to do well.
questions.next: If a marker spares a patient chemotherapy before surgery and the prediction is wrong, what does the residual disease in the specimen then commit her to?

questions.ask: What does leaving chemotherapy out before surgery commit a patient to after it?
questions.rationale: In this subtype the adjuvant decision is made on what is left in the specimen. Residual invasive disease sends a patient to a conjugate. A neoadjuvant regimen that raises the residual disease rate therefore does not take cytotoxic treatment out of the pathway. It moves it later. It also changes which agent is given and on what evidence that agent was chosen.
questions.experiment: The randomised comparison of two antibodies with endocrine therapy against the same antibodies with weekly paclitaxel reported response and then followed the same patients for invasive disease-free survival. The comparison of a conjugate against docetaxel and carboplatin did the same. Set against those are the post-neoadjuvant trials, which randomised patients with residual invasive disease to a conjugate against trastuzumab, and then to one conjugate against another. A further trial is testing whether escalation can be restricted by receptor and nodal status.
questions.finding: The chemotherapy-free arms leave more residual disease than their cytotoxic comparators do. They therefore send more patients into post-neoadjuvant escalation. In the endocrine comparison further chemotherapy was obligatory for anyone without a complete response, so the saving before surgery was spent again by protocol after it. Escalation with a conjugate is worth a great deal against trastuzumab alone. The newer conjugate is worth more again than the older one. The survival estimates in the endocrine comparison did not follow its response gap, on intervals too wide to settle the point in either direction.
questions.limitation: Nobody randomised the pathway as a whole. The neoadjuvant substitution trials were sized for response, so their survival curves are secondary. The post-neoadjuvant trials enrolled patients who arrived at residual disease after a cytotoxic backbone rather than after a chemotherapy-free one, so the benefit of escalation is being read across from a different upstream treatment. Residual disease left by a taxane is not obviously the same disease as residual disease left by endocrine therapy. The trial of the newer conjugate required nodal involvement in the surgical specimen, which is not the low-risk population a chemotherapy-free neoadjuvant course is aimed at. The trial that restricts escalation by receptor and nodal status has not reported.
questions.next: If post-neoadjuvant escalation is what carries the outcome in this subtype, should the neoadjuvant course be chosen to sort patients rather than to maximise response?

stories.title: Choosing what to add to preoperative chemotherapy, and what to take out
stories.premise: Treatment is given before surgery in this cell because the tumour answers back, sorting the population for everything that follows. So almost every question here is asked against pathological complete response, a measurement taken once at one operation. Almost every answer then has to survive the gap between that measurement and recurrence.

chapters.title: Selection by stage, and the price of treating everyone
Neoadjuvant therapy and checkpoint blockade

questions.ask: Does adding carboplatin to preoperative chemotherapy do more than raise pathological complete response?
questions.rationale: Triple-negative tumours are enriched for defective homologous recombination. Platinum works by making the interstrand crosslinks that this repair pathway exists to resolve. So a drug the rest of breast cancer has little use for should earn its place here. The preoperative setting is where that prediction could be read quickly.
questions.experiment: Randomised addition of carboplatin to a taxane and anthracycline backbone, in trials that differed in the backbone and in what else was randomised alongside it. The endpoint in each was pathological complete response. Later trials put the same addition against event-free or disease-free survival instead, giving the platinum before surgery, after it, or either way.
questions.finding: Carboplatin raised pathological complete response over the same backbone without it, in trial after trial. The trials that used survival rather than response as their endpoint found fewer events in the carboplatin arm. One of the response trials was followed for years afterwards and found no long-term advantage from the carboplatin it had added. One trial that set carboplatin against a different partner drug on the same taxane backbone saw its response advantage gone by the time survival was counted.
questions.limitation: These trials vary the platinum and the backbone together. The variable under test is not the platinum alone. They differ in which anthracycline was given, in whether a second experimental agent was randomised alongside in a factorial, and in how much of the planned chemotherapy survived the added toxicity. In the trial where the response advantage disappeared, treatment after the opening block of chemotherapy depended on how the tumour had responded. Its survival comparison is therefore confounded by what came next. One of the survival trials violated the proportional hazards assumption its summary estimate is computed under. That estimate does not describe the whole of its follow-up. Pathological complete response is also prognostic within an arm rather than a demonstrated surrogate across arms. The older trial that doubled it by adding a preoperative taxane, and changed no survival curve, is the standing demonstration of the difference.
questions.next: If the benefit comes from damage the tumour cannot repair, can the tumours that cannot repair it be identified before treatment starts?

questions.ask: Does a homologous recombination deficiency assay, or a germline BRCA mutation, identify who needs the platinum?
questions.rationale: If platinum works because a crosslink goes unrepaired, tumours that can repair one should not need it. A test for the defect would let the drug be allocated rather than given to everyone. That matters here because platinum toxicity is what limits delivery of the rest of the regimen.
questions.experiment: Two randomised trials built around the marker rather than around the drug. One set single-agent platinum against a single-agent taxane, and asked whether a deficiency score above a fixed cut-point predicted response to the platinum specifically. The other set single-agent platinum against an anthracycline regimen in germline carriers. A third trial selected patients by the deficiency assay and put a PARP inhibitor in the platinum's place. A single-arm window study gave a PARP inhibitor to patients selected for none of this.
questions.finding: The deficiency score did not separate response to platinum from response to a taxane. In germline carriers, platinum produced no more complete responses than the anthracycline regimen those patients would have had anyway. Selecting on the assay did not make the platinum-free arm clear the response threshold set for it. Unselected tumours given a PARP inhibitor responded often enough to make the marker look less like a gate than a description.
questions.limitation: The biomarker trial was sized to test a predictive claim rather than to compare two drugs. Its arm-to-arm difference is not an efficacy result. A large share of its patients crossed to another preoperative regimen before surgery. The assay could not be scored on all of the rest. Entry to the germline trial required a mutation rather than triple-negative disease. Hormone receptor-positive patients therefore sit inside its answer. The assay-selected trial tested one arm against a fixed threshold rather than against its comparator. Its arms can be described and not compared. No trial here kept an assay-negative arm on the same treatment, which is the comparison that would show what the selection bought.
questions.next: If the assay cannot allocate the platinum, can it allocate a PARP inhibitor? And can that drug replace the chemotherapy rather than join it?

questions.ask: Can a PARP inhibitor stand in for the chemotherapy before surgery rather than be added to it?
questions.rationale: A PARP inhibitor kills cells that cannot repair a double-strand break. That is the same vulnerability the platinum is aimed at. If the oral drug does that work, the case for the cytotoxic backbone weakens. Its toxicity is of a different kind, which is the whole appeal in a disease being treated for cure.
questions.experiment: The designs run from addition to replacement. One trial randomised a PARP inhibitor on top of a platinum and taxane backbone, with a third arm carrying neither. One substituted the PARP inhibitor for the platinum in assay-selected patients. Two gave a PARP inhibitor as the only preoperative treatment, one for a full course in germline carriers, one as a short window before the chemotherapy in unselected disease. A further single-arm study pairs a PARP inhibitor with a checkpoint inhibitor and no chemotherapy at all.
questions.finding: Added to a platinum-containing backbone, the PARP inhibitor added nothing to it. Substituted for the platinum in selected patients, it did not clear the response threshold the trial had set itself, although it landed near the platinum arm. Given alone for a full course in germline carriers, it cleared tumours at a rate close to what combination chemotherapy achieves, and still fell short of its own prespecified bar. A short window of it, in patients unselected for a repair defect, produced objective responses in many of the tumours it was given to.
questions.limitation: The addition trial used a PARP inhibitor that traps the enzyme on DNA weakly. A null result there is a result about one molecule rather than about the class. The monotherapy trials are single-arm. Their response rates have no concurrent comparator, so they get read against chemotherapy rates from other trials in other populations. One of them reports its response on an evaluable denominator rather than on everyone enrolled. A window of a few weeks followed by planned chemotherapy says nothing about whether that chemotherapy could have been left out. The chemotherapy-free combination has no PARP-only arm. Nothing in it separates the checkpoint inhibitor's contribution from the PARP inhibitor's.
questions.next: If chemotherapy is to come out, the other candidate for carrying the treatment is the immune response. Does adding a checkpoint inhibitor before surgery lower recurrence?

questions.ask: Does adding a checkpoint inhibitor to preoperative chemotherapy lower recurrence, and does it have to be given before surgery?
questions.rationale: Triple-negative tumours carry more tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and more neoantigen than the other subtypes. Chemotherapy releases antigen as it kills. A checkpoint inhibitor given while the primary tumour and its draining nodes are still in place should prime a wider response than one given to a patient who has neither left.
questions.experiment: Several randomised additions of a checkpoint inhibitor to preoperative chemotherapy. They differ in the drug, in whether the backbone carried a platinum, and in whether the checkpoint inhibitor continued after surgery. Set against them, two trials gave a checkpoint inhibitor only after surgery, with no preoperative phase at all. A further trial is randomising the omission of the post-surgical half in patients whose tumours cleared.
questions.finding: Adding a checkpoint inhibitor raised pathological complete response over the same chemotherapy with placebo in most of these trials. In the trial that also continued it after surgery, the event-free survival advantage held. A large trial of a different checkpoint inhibitor, given across both halves of the pathway, missed its primary endpoint. Both trials that waited until after surgery were negative on their primary endpoints.
questions.limitation: The practice-defining trial varies more than the checkpoint inhibitor. Its backbone carries a platinum. Its treatment continues after surgery. Neither of those was randomised separately. The trial cannot say which part is load-bearing. The trial that ran no post-surgical phase reported a survival separation its own response endpoint did not support, on few events. Checkpoint ligand expression did not select here the way it does in metastatic disease. The co-primary analysis in the marker-positive population did not cross its significance boundary. The assay and its cut-point differ between these trials in any case. The adjuvant-only trials differ in drug and in population as well as in timing. The case for the preoperative window is therefore drawn between trials rather than inside one. Whether the post-surgical half is needed at all is only now being randomised. That trial has not reported.
questions.next: If the parts of the package were never randomised against each other, the first one to take out is the cytotoxic backbone. How much chemotherapy still has to sit underneath the checkpoint inhibitor?

questions.ask: How much chemotherapy still has to sit underneath the checkpoint inhibitor?
questions.rationale: The cytotoxic part of the regimen carries the cardiac risk, the leukaemia risk and most of the acute toxicity. If the platinum and the immune agent are doing the work, the anthracycline is a cost with nothing on the other side of it. Taken further, the same argument asks whether any chemotherapy is needed in a tumour that already has an immune infiltrate.
questions.experiment: One randomised comparison set an anthracycline-free platinum and taxane regimen against the same drugs followed by an anthracycline, with response as the endpoint. A single-arm study gave that short regimen with a checkpoint inhibitor added. One trial kept the anthracycline but moved it after surgery, and randomised the checkpoint inhibitor on what was left in front. A randomised trial of the short regimen against the standard one, with event-free survival as its endpoint, is running. At the far end, a chemotherapy-free trial gave checkpoint blockade alone to tumours selected by a lymphocyte cut-point.
questions.finding: Anthracycline-free regimens reach response rates close to those of the anthracycline-containing ones. Where the anthracycline was deferred until after surgery, the checkpoint inhibitor's response advantage did not appear. Checkpoint blockade with no chemotherapy at all cleared some lymphocyte-rich tumours completely. It did so at the price of frequent immune endocrinopathy in patients who were otherwise well.
questions.limitation: All of these read out at the operation. The one trial randomising the two regimens against an outcome has not reported. The anthracycline-free comparison is small and was powered for response, which is the endpoint already shown in this cell to move without survival moving with it. The version that added the checkpoint inhibitor to that short regimen is single-arm. Its response rate has no concurrent standard-regimen control to be set against. The trial that deferred the anthracycline has published only a secondary response endpoint. It cannot be used to argue that the anthracycline was the missing ingredient. The chemotherapy-free trial ran window cohorts whose endpoint is a laboratory measure of immune activation. Only its selected surgical cohort carried a response endpoint. A lymphocyte score read on one slide against a percentage cut-point is a scoring convention rather than a property of the tumour. That trial selected on it.
questions.next: If response at the operation cannot license taking a drug out, what can a preoperative trial settle at all, and what has to wait for a randomised outcome trial?

questions.ask: What can a preoperative trial settle about a new drug, and what has to wait for a randomised trial after surgery?
questions.rationale: The preoperative window is the fastest read in this disease. The tumour is still in place. The endpoint arrives at the operation. Paired biopsies make the mechanism visible. So it is the natural place to try a conjugate, a targeted addition or a physical primer, well before anyone commits to a trial with survival as its endpoint.
questions.experiment: An adaptive platform runs candidate agents against a shared chemotherapy control and graduates them on a Bayesian probability of success in a future trial. A conjugate was given alone in a single arm, with treatment after those cycles left to the treating physician. A JAK inhibitor was added to preoperative chemotherapy in inflammatory triple-negative disease, with a pharmacodynamic conversion as the primary endpoint. Preoperative radiation dose was randomised as an immune primer, with immunological endpoints. The randomised conjugate trials in this disease all sit after surgery, in patients with residual disease.
questions.finding: Conjugate monotherapy cleared a minority of untreated tumours. That is enough to say the class is active before surgery. It is not enough to say it belongs there. The JAK inhibitor lowered its pathway marker in the biopsies taken after the short run-in. Sustained dosing alongside the taxane raised the same signalling rather than lowering it. Response in that rare population stayed low.
questions.limitation: A graduation probability is a prediction about a trial not yet done rather than a result. The conjugate trial is single-arm and response-guided. What patients received after those cycles was at their physician's discretion. Its event-free survival therefore describes a pathway rather than a drug. The inflammatory trial enrolled very few patients. Its response figure rests on a handful of events. Its own primary endpoint was a pharmacodynamic conversion proportion, and the published report never states that proportion. Its run-in sits inside the randomisation rather than before it, so its two comparisons overlap. The radiation trial's endpoints are immunological. Its dose comparisons are exploratory and do not rank doses for efficacy. None of the randomised conjugate trials asks a preoperative question. There is no randomised basis for moving one in front of surgery.
questions.next: Does the conjugate stay behind surgery, where the residual-disease trials are already randomising it, or is a preoperative comparison against the standard regimen worth mounting first?

questions.ask: Does the taxane formulation change what the preoperative window shows?
questions.rationale: Nab-paclitaxel removes the solvent that limits how much paclitaxel can be given and changes how the drug reaches the tumour. A higher delivered dose without the solvent was expected to raise the response rate, and the preoperative setting measures response directly.
questions.experiment: Randomisation of nab-paclitaxel against paclitaxel, each for four cycles before an anthracycline regimen, in HER2-negative early or locally advanced disease, with pathological complete response as the endpoint.
questions.finding: The pathological complete response rate was not improved.
questions.limitation: The trial enrolled HER2-negative disease rather than this subtype alone, so the result is an average over two populations whose response rates differ by a factor of several. A negative result on response does not establish that the two formulations are equivalent on toxicity, which is the axis on which the choice is usually made.
questions.next: If the formulation does not change response, does it change who can complete the regimen?

stories.title: Allocating further treatment on what surgery finds
stories.premise: Nearly every stage II or III triple-negative cancer now meets chemotherapy before it meets a surgeon, which makes the operation a report on the drugs as well as a removal of the tumour. That report splits the population in two: a pathological complete response that rarely relapses, and residual invasive disease that carries most of the events and carries them early. Every question at this position is therefore about what to add, to whom, and on the strength of which measurement.

chapters.title: Selection by stage, and the price of treating everyone
Neoadjuvant therapy and checkpoint blockade
Adjuvant and post-neoadjuvant therapy

questions.ask: Does what surgery finds after neoadjuvant treatment identify who needs more treatment?
questions.rationale: Giving the same chemotherapy before surgery rather than after it does not change survival. The reason to give it first is that surgery then reports whether the drugs worked. In triple-negative disease that report separates the population more sharply than anything measurable before treatment. A complete response is common in this subtype. Residual invasive disease relapses within a few years of surgery rather than over the decades that hormone receptor-positive disease can take.
questions.experiment: The foundational trials randomised the timing of chemotherapy, and then the addition of a taxane to the preoperative course, with survival as the endpoint and pathological response recorded alongside. A platform trial read response against outcome across its molecular subtypes on a shared chemotherapy control. Randomised trials that added carboplatin to preoperative chemotherapy reported the response rate first and their survival endpoints years later. The registration trial for chemo-immunotherapy carried both endpoints inside one randomisation.
questions.finding: Response sorts the population steeply. Patients who clear the breast and the axilla relapse rarely. Residual disease accounts for most of the events. That sorting is prognostic within an arm. It has repeatedly failed to behave as a surrogate between arms. Carboplatin raised the response rate over the same chemotherapy without it, and the later outcome analyses of those same trials found no gain. Where a trial moved both endpoints together, that is agreement rather than evidence that the first predicts the second.
questions.limitation: The timing trials enrolled all comers before subtype was routinely recorded. The response gradient they established is being read into a subtype they did not define. What counts as a complete response is a convention rather than a fact. The trials differ on whether residual in-situ disease disqualifies it. Residual cancer burden grades what that dichotomy discards. What the pathologist reports also depends on how the specimen and the post-chemotherapy axilla were sampled. Residual disease marks resistance to the regimen that was actually given. It says nothing about drugs the tumour never met.
questions.next: If residual disease marks the population carrying the events, does giving those patients a further course of a different chemotherapy lower recurrence?

questions.ask: Does a further course of chemotherapy after surgery lower recurrence in residual triple-negative disease?
questions.rationale: A tumour still present after a full anthracycline and taxane course has demonstrated resistance to both classes in the patient it is growing in. The interval before relapse is short. Anything that will work has to be given now. A fluoropyrimidine is not cross-resistant with either class. It is tolerable enough to start soon after surgery.
questions.experiment: Residual HER2-negative disease after neoadjuvant anthracycline, taxane or both was randomised to capecitabine or to no further chemotherapy, with disease-free survival as the endpoint. The same drug was tested separately in populations selected by stage rather than by response. One of those trials gave a conventional course after standard adjuvant chemotherapy. The other gave a metronomic year.
questions.finding: Capecitabine for residual disease lowered recurrence and death against no further chemotherapy. The effect was larger in the triple-negative subgroup than in the hormone receptor-positive one. In the populations selected by stage rather than by response the same drug missed its endpoint in one trial and met it in the other. Those two differed in dose, schedule and duration.
questions.limitation: The residual disease trial stopped early at an interim analysis that had met its endpoint, which is the circumstance in which an effect is most likely to be overstated. Its triple-negative result is a subgroup of a HER2-negative trial rather than a trial in this subtype. It was run where neither carboplatin nor a checkpoint inhibitor formed part of neoadjuvant treatment. Its control arm is therefore a patient nobody now treats. The basal and non-basal gradient reported in the trial that selected by stage is an interaction test on a centrally scored phenotype, not a randomised allocation by that phenotype.
questions.next: If a fluoropyrimidine is the benchmark, is it the right cytotoxic, or would a platinum do better against tumours selected for having survived a taxane?

questions.ask: Is a platinum a better post-neoadjuvant cytotoxic than capecitabine for residual disease?
questions.rationale: Triple-negative tumours carry defects in homologous recombination often enough to give a DNA-crosslinking agent a mechanistic claim on them. Adding carboplatin before surgery raises the pathological response rate over the same chemotherapy without it. If it works on the tumour while it is still in the breast, it ought to work on what is left of it.
questions.experiment: Residual disease above a size threshold was randomised to a platinum or to capecitabine, as a non-inferiority design. Subtype was assigned by a multigene classifier run on the residual tissue. The primary comparison was prespecified in the basal group.
questions.finding: Platinum did not prove non-inferior to capecitabine. The estimate ran against it. Severe toxicity was more common with platinum than with capecitabine. The monitoring committee closed the trial well short of its planned enrolment. Outcome was poor in both arms.
questions.limitation: A non-inferiority trial closed before it has its events can show neither non-inferiority nor inferiority. This one read a fraction of the information it was designed for. An estimate that had looked similar between the arms would not have settled the question either. The classifier was run on tissue that had already been through chemotherapy. The subtype defining the analysis population is therefore a measurement made after selection rather than a property of the tumour that was enrolled. The size threshold narrows the population further. Residual disease below that threshold is not represented. The case for platinum came from trials in chemotherapy-naive tumours, which is precisely the extrapolation at issue.
questions.next: If choosing the cytotoxic by histology has run out, does choosing a drug by the tumour's inherited genotype do better?

questions.ask: Does a PARP inhibitor lower recurrence in germline BRCA carriers left with residual disease?
questions.rationale: A germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 loss is a repair defect the tumour cannot work around. PARP inhibition is lethal in that background. Carriers are over-represented in triple-negative disease. The carriers at highest risk are the ones whose tumours survived neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
questions.experiment: High-risk HER2-negative germline carriers were randomised after local treatment and chemotherapy to a year of olaparib or to placebo, with invasive disease-free survival as the endpoint. High risk was met either by residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy or by stage in patients who had surgery first.
questions.finding: Olaparib lowered invasive and distant recurrence against placebo. The advantage held on longer follow-up. It became an overall survival difference as well.
questions.limitation: The two routes into the trial are not one population. The trial was not designed to separate them. What the drug is worth specifically in residual triple-negative disease is therefore an inference from a stratified trial rather than a result of it. Selection was germline, which leaves outside the result the larger group of triple-negative tumours with a BRCA-like phenotype and no inherited variant. Attempts to identify that group by a repair-deficiency score have not predicted response to a platinum. In carriers themselves a platinum did not outperform an anthracycline regimen before surgery. The genotype does not simply mean platinum sensitivity. Enrolment also largely preceded the checkpoint inhibitor. Nothing here says how olaparib sits alongside adjuvant pembrolizumab or alongside capecitabine.
questions.next: Since every benchmark at this position was set before the checkpoint inhibitor entered neoadjuvant treatment, does that drug have to continue after surgery at all?

questions.ask: Does checkpoint blockade have to continue after surgery?
questions.rationale: The registration trial gave pembrolizumab before and after surgery inside a single randomisation. It cannot say which half of the schedule produced the benefit. There is reason to think the halves are not equivalent. Before surgery the antigen and the infiltrating lymphocytes are still in the breast. Afterwards they are not. The adjuvant phase also adds exposure to a class of toxicity that does not resolve when the drug is stopped.
questions.experiment: One trial added an antibody to adjuvant chemotherapy in patients operated first. Another gave a year of a different antibody after surgery in high-risk disease, with a residual disease stratum as a co-primary population. A third continued its antibody across surgery on a carboplatin-containing neoadjuvant backbone. A fourth randomises omission of the adjuvant phase in patients who achieved a complete response.
questions.finding: Checkpoint blockade begun after surgery has not lowered recurrence. The trial in patients operated first was halted for futility with its estimate on the wrong side of no difference. The trial with the residual disease stratum missed both co-primary endpoints. The trial that continued its antibody across surgery missed its primary endpoint as well. The omission trial has not reported.
questions.limitation: None of the reported trials asked what the clinic asks, which is whether the adjuvant phase can be dropped in a patient who has already had the neoadjuvant phase. The unreported omission trial asks it only in patients with a complete response. Residual disease is left where it started. The reported trials use different antibodies on different chemotherapy backbones. They are not replicates of one another. A negative result in one does not transfer to another. The survival comparison favouring avelumab was descriptive and sat outside the testing hierarchy. It is not a positive result recovered from a negative trial. The trial that continued its antibody across surgery had carboplatin in both arms. Nothing in it separates the antibody from its backbone.
questions.next: If the adjuvant checkpoint inhibitor now sits inside the control arm of every residual disease trial, can a new drug class beat that control?

questions.ask: Can an antibody-drug conjugate displace capecitabine as the treatment for residual disease?
questions.rationale: The capecitabine benchmark was set in patients who had received neither carboplatin nor a checkpoint inhibitor. The group left with residual disease today has survived more treatment than the group in which that benchmark was measured. Conjugates deliver a topoisomerase-I payload to antigens expressed on most triple-negative tumours. They work in pretreated metastatic disease. Residual disease is the earliest point at which that activity can be aimed at a population still curable.
questions.experiment: One randomised trial gives a conjugate with a checkpoint inhibitor against a physician's choice arm of the checkpoint inhibitor with or without capecitabine. Another gives a different conjugate, alone or with a checkpoint inhibitor, against investigator's choice of capecitabine, a checkpoint inhibitor or both. A third compares a conjugate against physician's choice in residual HER2-negative disease, in separate hormone receptor-positive and triple-negative cohorts. A single-arm neoadjuvant study had already shown that a conjugate alone produces pathological responses in untreated disease.
questions.finding: None of the randomised trials has reported. What is on the record is design, rationale and a single-arm response signal in untreated disease. It should be read as that and nothing more.
questions.limitation: A design paper is not an efficacy result and must never be cited as one. The comparator in each randomised trial is a choice rather than a fixed regimen. The control is therefore a mixture that will drift as practice drifts. A difference against it is harder to attribute than a difference against a named drug. The trial spanning hormone receptor-positive and triple-negative residual disease has to be read by cohort, because the two differ in biology and in what their choice arm is likely to contain. The single-arm study left subsequent systemic treatment to the treating physician. Its later outcomes describe a whole pathway rather than the conjugate.
questions.next: If a conjugate, a PARP inhibitor and a checkpoint inhibitor each prove themselves against a control arm that contained neither of the other two, on what evidence does a clinic give one carrier with residual disease all three?

questions.ask: What is the cytotoxic backbone that everything else in this subtype is added to?
questions.rationale: In the other two subtypes chemotherapy is the thing being spared. Here it is the backbone, and every addition tested in this part is an addition to it. What that backbone should be was settled in trials enrolled without regard to receptor status, which is the reason it is rarely stated explicitly in a chapter about this subtype.
questions.experiment: Randomised additions, substitutions and schedule changes on an anthracycline and taxane combination, mostly in unselected populations. Separately, within this subtype, a platinum and taxane regimen randomised against an anthracycline-containing one, and a nab-paclitaxel substitution tested preoperatively in HER2-negative disease.
questions.finding: The taxane addition and the shortened interval hold. Within this subtype specifically, replacing the anthracycline with a platinum improved disease-free survival in one trial. Substituting nab-paclitaxel for paclitaxel did not raise the pathological complete response rate, and substituting capecitabine for standard chemotherapy in older patients was worse.
questions.limitation: The generalisable part of this record was not randomised within this subtype, and the part that was comes from a single trial in one population. That trial compared its regimen against a control arm predating checkpoint blockade. The question it answers is not the question a clinic now asks.
questions.next: If the backbone changes because immunotherapy is now added to it, does the platinum comparison have to be run again?

stories.title: Finding disease that no scan can see, and having nothing to give for it
stories.premise: A blood test identifies, years ahead, the patients whose disease will come back. No treatment has been shown to change what happens to them. Every question in this position is a version of the gap between those two sentences, and the honest state of the field is that the gap is still open.

chapters.title: Molecular residual disease

questions.ask: How reliably does a blood assay identify the patients who will relapse?
questions.rationale: Recurrence after curative treatment arrives from disease that was present at surgery and invisible to every imaging modality. A plasma assay that detects it would convert an unobservable state into an observable one.
questions.experiment: Prospective cohorts followed with serial plasma sampling after curative-intent treatment, using personalised assays built from the resected tumour. Separately, a surveillance programme that sampled at fixed intervals and recorded what it missed as well as what it found.
questions.finding: Detection is among the strongest prognostic separations reported for any biomarker in this disease, and it arrives well before clinical relapse. The warning interval differs by subtype.
questions.limitation: A cohort assembled around a test measures the test. None of these designs randomised anything, so they establish that detection predicts relapse and nothing about whether detecting it helps. Patients who relapsed with no prior detection at all are the part of the record most often left out of the summary.
questions.next: If the test identifies the right patients, is there anything to give them?

questions.ask: Is plasma the only compartment worth sampling?
questions.rationale: Disseminated tumour cells in marrow are the older observation and the more direct one. A marrow aspirate finds the cells themselves rather than fragments of the DNA they shed, and shedding requires turnover that a dormant cell may not have.
questions.experiment: Bone marrow aspiration to find disseminated tumour cells directly, in survivors within five years of diagnosis, followed by randomised treatment allocation among those found positive.
questions.finding: Marrow disease can be found, treated and reduced, and the trial that did so was feasible and tolerable. It was not designed to show a recurrence benefit and it did not claim one.
questions.limitation: No trial randomises one compartment against the other, so the field treats marrow and plasma as two routes to one state on an assumption rather than a finding. Marrow aspiration is also a procedure rather than a blood draw, which limits how often it can be repeated.
questions.next: If the two compartments identify different patients, which of them names the population an intervention should be tested in?

questions.ask: Does treating molecularly detected disease change what happens next?
questions.rationale: The advanced setting has shown twice that acting on a molecular signal before radiological progression can buy time. The same logic applied after curative treatment would intercept recurrence rather than delay it.
questions.experiment: Three different drug classes offered to patients who became positive on surveillance. Checkpoint blockade in triple-negative disease, autophagy and mTOR inhibition against marrow disease, and endocrine escalation in hormone receptor-positive disease.
questions.finding: Nothing has yet shown that treatment changes the outcome. The one trial that reported a therapeutic result found that most patients already had metastases on imaging when the assay turned positive, and that the drug cleared the assay in nobody.
questions.limitation: Each of these trials chose its class on an argument rather than on a precedent, and the arguments are not compatible with each other. Checkpoint blockade assumes the cells are proliferating enough to be seen and dormancy-directed treatment assumes they are not proliferating at all. A negative trial therefore cannot be read as a statement about the setting.
questions.next: Were these trials testing the wrong drug, or surveilling at the wrong time?

questions.ask: Does running a surveillance programme help the population it is run on?
questions.rationale: A test is only worth sending if the strategy built around it improves outcomes, and lead time by itself moves the date of diagnosis without moving the date of death.
questions.experiment: Randomisation of the surveillance strategy itself rather than of the treatment given to those it finds, so that the comparison is between a followed population and a conventionally followed one.
questions.finding: No result. The designs that ask this question in its randomised form have not reported.
questions.limitation: This is the question a clinic needs answered and the hardest one to fund, because it requires enrolling everyone to study the few who become positive. A trial that randomises treatment among test-positive patients is a cheaper design that answers a different question.
questions.next: If a programme does help, does the benefit come from the earlier treatment or from the earlier imaging that followed the positive result?

stories.title: Choosing the first-line regimen and the moment to leave it
stories.premise: At this point almost every patient has a first option that works and is tolerable. Because the disease is still incurable, the drug that is not given now will usually be given later. That makes the arguments here about allocation rather than about activity: what belongs in the first regimen, what can be held back for the second, and what signal should end the first line.

chapters.title: Endocrine resistance, and the presentations the sequence does not fit
Endocrine therapy and receptor degraders after progression
CDK4/6 inhibition, combinations and sequencing

questions.ask: Does adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to first-line endocrine therapy do more than endocrine therapy alone?
questions.rationale: Oestrogen drives proliferation through cyclin D and the CDK4 and CDK6 kinases. The receptor and the cell cycle therefore sit on one line. Endocrine monotherapy holds first-line disease for a while and then stops holding it. Blocking the kinases downstream of the receptor was expected to deepen that control and to delay the escape rather than to work around it.
questions.experiment: Placebo-controlled addition of an inhibitor to the endocrine therapy the patient would have received anyway, in endocrine-sensitive disease untreated for the advanced stage. The trials differ in the agent, in the endocrine partner, and in whether the population was postmenopausal or premenopausal with ovarian suppression.
questions.finding: Every one of these trials lengthened time to progression against the same endocrine therapy given alone. The progression results sit close enough together across the agents in wide use to read as one class effect. Survival was a secondary endpoint in all of them. The class claim therefore rests on progression alone.
questions.limitation: No trial here compared one inhibitor with another. Any ranking of the agents is therefore a set of across-trial contrasts and not a randomised comparison. None of these trials carried overall survival as its primary endpoint, which makes every survival result a secondary one from a trial powered for progression. They also differ in endocrine partner, in enrolment year and in what patients were allowed afterwards. One of them enrolled a population mixing first and second line, which makes it speak less cleanly to this question than the rest. A fourth agent enters the class on a single trial of its own. What reads as a class effect is therefore far better evidenced for some agents than for others.
questions.next: If the combination beats endocrine therapy alone in the first line, is that because the inhibitor was given first, or only because it was given at all?

questions.ask: Does the CDK4/6 inhibitor have to be given in the first line, or can it be held back for the second?
questions.rationale: The first-line trials compared a regimen containing the inhibitor against one without it. That is not the choice a clinic faces, because almost every patient will receive the drug at some point. What is being chosen is where in the sequence to spend it. Spending it first commits the patient to continuous treatment and monitoring while the disease is still endocrine-sensitive.
questions.experiment: One randomised trial allocated untreated advanced disease to two strategies rather than to two drugs. One arm gave the inhibitor with an aromatase inhibitor first and endocrine monotherapy second. The other gave endocrine monotherapy first and the inhibitor with fulvestrant second. The endpoint ran from randomisation to the second progression, because any within-line endpoint would necessarily favour the arm given two drugs first.
questions.finding: Neither the across-line endpoint nor overall survival separated the two strategies. The early strategy delivered far more inhibitor exposure than the deferred one, and more high-grade toxicity with it.
questions.limitation: The endpoint that makes this a strategy trial also stops it answering a within-line question. Nothing in it contradicts the first-line trials on their own terms. The protocol did not fix which inhibitor was used. The result travels only as far as the agents patients were actually given. The second-line evidence standing behind the deferred arm comes from trials run in patients who had not had an inhibitor in the first line, which is not the position a deferred patient is in today. The trial set no requirement about how fast the disease was moving. It says nothing about the patient who needs a response now.
questions.next: If deferral costs nothing on average, does it cost something in the patient whose disease is moving fast enough that chemotherapy is being considered?

questions.ask: Can endocrine therapy with a CDK4/6 inhibitor replace chemotherapy when the disease is moving fast?
questions.rationale: Aggressive visceral disease is where clinicians reach for chemotherapy first, on the belief that only cytotoxic treatment produces a response quickly enough to matter. That belief was formed against the slow and partial responses of endocrine monotherapy. The combination is not endocrine monotherapy, which is reason enough to test the belief rather than carry it forward.
questions.experiment: A randomised comparison of ribociclib with endocrine therapy against investigator's choice combination chemotherapy, in first-line disease the investigator judged aggressive enough to warrant chemotherapy. Alongside it, two trials set an inhibitor with endocrine therapy against capecitabine, one in premenopausal patients with ovarian suppression and one in aromatase inhibitor-resistant disease. A further trial randomises immediate abemaciclib with endocrine therapy against a short course of paclitaxel given before the same combination.
questions.finding: In aggressive first-line disease the endocrine combination held the disease longer than combination chemotherapy did. Against capecitabine the answer depends on the population. In premenopausal patients with ovarian suppression the combination lengthened time to progression against capecitabine. In aromatase inhibitor-resistant disease it did not beat capecitabine.
questions.limitation: The aggressive-disease trial was a phase II. Its comparator was a combination chemotherapy regimen rather than the sequential single agents many clinics would use, which is a comparator chosen for toxicity as much as for efficacy. Its endpoint was progression-free survival and not the speed of response on which the practice it challenges actually rests. Entry turned on the investigator's judgement that chemotherapy was indicated rather than on a stated visceral crisis threshold. That makes the population a product of a decision rather than of a measurement, which no protocol can reproduce. Of the two capecitabine trials, one enrolled a population only half of whom were untreated for metastatic disease. The other was not first line at all. The induction trial has no verified peer-reviewed result on the record. Nothing about giving chemotherapy before the combination can be read from it yet. An early response to induction would in any case not be an answer for every urgent presentation. Its eligibility and its exact sequence have to travel with it whenever it is cited.
questions.next: If the endocrine combination can carry disease this aggressive, is an aromatase inhibitor still the right endocrine half of it?

questions.ask: Which endocrine partner should the first-line inhibitor be given with?
questions.rationale: An aromatase inhibitor lowers the ligand and leaves the receptor standing. A degrader removes the receptor itself, which should matter more as the receptor rather than the ligand becomes the limiting step. The comparison is an old one. It was asked in a backbone that no longer exists in clinic.
questions.experiment: Fulvestrant was compared with anastrozole as first-line monotherapy in endocrine-naive advanced disease, first in a phase II and then in a phase III. Two further trials added fulvestrant to anastrozole instead of substituting it. A separate randomised comparison of two fulvestrant doses settled the dose, after the addition trials had already been designed. Three phase III trials now put an oral degrader against an aromatase inhibitor with the same CDK4/6 inhibitor in both arms, which is the substitution question asked in the backbone actually used.
questions.finding: Substituting fulvestrant for the aromatase inhibitor lengthened progression-free survival in endocrine-naive disease in the phase III. The phase II that preceded it did not meet its own clinical benefit endpoint. Adding fulvestrant to anastrozole gave a gain in one trial and nothing in the other. The three degrader trials with an inhibitor in both arms have not reported.
questions.limitation: Every reported trial in this comparison used an endocrine backbone with no CDK4/6 inhibitor in it. They answer a question about monotherapy and not about the combination now given. The two addition trials disagree. They also differ in how much adjuvant endocrine therapy their populations had already had, which is an explanation for the disagreement that is not the drug. Both used the lower fulvestrant dose, which the dose comparison later showed was the wrong one. The addition question was therefore asked at a dose nobody now prescribes. The phase II's survival analysis was added by protocol amendment after the progression results were known, which makes it something other than a prespecified comparison.
questions.next: If the aromatase inhibitor is the part of the backbone under which the receptor mutates, should it be replaced when the mutation appears rather than at the start for everyone?

questions.ask: Should a rising ESR1 mutation end the first line before the scan does?
questions.rationale: ESR1 mutations are selected by oestrogen deprivation and leave the receptor active without ligand, which is why an aromatase inhibitor stops working while a degrader still has a target. The mutation is detectable in blood before the scan changes. That interval is an opportunity if acting inside it changes anything, and a source of premature treatment change if it does not.
questions.experiment: Two trials sampled blood serially during first-line treatment and randomised only those patients whose ESR1 mutation rose while the disease was still controlled radiologically. One swapped the aromatase inhibitor for fulvestrant and kept palbociclib. The other swapped it for an oral degrader and kept whichever inhibitor the patient was already taking. Both left the control arm on the aromatase inhibitor the tumour had already learned to ignore.
questions.finding: Switching at the molecular signal lengthened progression-free survival measured from that randomisation in both trials. The receptor-directed drugs tested after clinical progression point the same way and show the same dependence on ESR1 status, which is what makes the mechanism credible rather than the timing.
questions.limitation: Neither trial randomised the comparison a clinic actually weighs, which is making the same switch at clinical progression. The control arm continued a treatment already known at the molecular level to be failing. The contrast is therefore against something close to inert. The endpoint is progression on the new line measured from the molecular randomisation, which is a surrogate for what the strategy is worth across the whole line and a clock that starts at a point chosen by an assay. The population is defined by that assay and its threshold, which makes molecular progression here a laboratory convention as much as a biological event. Patients whose resistance takes another route never enter. An earlier trial that switched treatment on a persistent blood marker rather than on a scan did not improve survival, which is the reason this design needs an outcome and not only a progression result.
questions.next: If a resistance mechanism that appears during treatment can be acted on before it causes progression, should an alteration present from the start change the first regimen itself?

questions.ask: Should the first-line regimen be chosen by the tumour's pathway alterations rather than given as one combination to everyone?
questions.rationale: PIK3CA, AKT1 and PTEN alterations mark disease that escapes endocrine control early. A germline BRCA mutation marks a repair defect that a different class exploits. Both have been treated as later-line problems, addressed once the standard first line has failed. If the alteration is already there at presentation, waiting for it to cause progression spends the best line of treatment on a regimen the tumour is equipped to escape.
questions.experiment: One trial took patients whose disease relapsed on adjuvant endocrine therapy or soon after finishing it and whose tumour carried a PIK3CA mutation. It added a PI3K-alpha inhibitor to palbociclib with fulvestrant against the same doublet with placebo. Trials of AKT inhibition added to an inhibitor with fulvestrant, and of a PARP1-selective inhibitor with a degrader replacing the inhibitor in germline BRCA-mutated disease, are running. The pathway drugs themselves were established after progression, each added to fulvestrant and read out in a marker-defined population.
questions.finding: Adding the PI3K-alpha inhibitor to the first-line doublet lengthened both progression-free and overall survival in that selected population. The later-line trials of the same pathway established a progression benefit in marker-defined disease without establishing a survival benefit. Selection by anything other than a PIK3CA mutation is so far a design rather than a result.
questions.limitation: The first-line triplet population was selected twice, by the mutation and by relapse on adjuvant endocrine therapy or shortly after it. It is a narrow and unusually resistant slice of the first line. The result does not transfer to a mutation-positive patient with a long treatment-free interval. No trial has tested it in one. The comparison is a triplet against a doublet, which puts added toxicity into what is being traded. No arm isolates the pathway inhibitor from the cell cycle drug. No arm held the pathway inhibitor back to progression either. First-line intensification has therefore never been compared with the same drug given later, which is the question the deferral trial asked of the CDK4/6 inhibitor.
questions.next: Does first-line intensification by biology survive the test that was applied to the CDK4/6 inhibitor, an endpoint that runs across both lines rather than within the first?

stories.title: Choosing the next treatment after CDK4/6 inhibition fails
stories.premise: Everyone who reaches this position has already had a CDK4/6 inhibitor with endocrine therapy, which settles the question of whether to give one. What is left to work out is what the disease has become on it: an oestrogen receptor rewritten so that it works without its ligand, a parallel pathway carrying the proliferative signal, or a clone that has stopped depending on oestrogen at all. The questions run in that order, from what to change inside the endocrine regimen to when to abandon it.

chapters.title: Endocrine resistance, and the presentations the sequence does not fit
Endocrine therapy and receptor degraders after progression
CDK4/6 inhibition, combinations and sequencing
Conjugates and chemotherapy in later lines
Metastatic therapy from first line onwards

questions.ask: Is there anything left to gain from CDK4/6 inhibition after the disease has progressed on a CDK4/6 inhibitor?
questions.rationale: Resistance to this class is rarely the loss of its target. Retinoblastoma protein is still expressed in most tumours that progress. Much of what fails is the endocrine half of the combination. If that is right, the kinase is still worth blocking. What needs changing is the receptor.
questions.experiment: Four randomised trials gave a CDK4/6 inhibitor with endocrine therapy after progression on one, against the same endocrine therapy alone. Two switched to a different inhibitor from the one that had failed. Two continued or restarted the one that had failed. Two single-arm studies asked the same thing with no control. One rechallenged with the failed inhibitor and a changed endocrine partner. The other gave a CDK4/6 inhibitor, an mTOR inhibitor and a steroidal aromatase inhibitor together.
questions.finding: The two trials that switched the inhibitor lengthened progression-free survival against endocrine therapy alone. Neither trial that kept the failed inhibitor did, whether it was continued without a break or restarted after one. Both single-arm studies met their own clinical benefit thresholds. Those thresholds were set against no comparator. Where a randomised gain exists it is small beside what this class bought when it was given in the first line.
questions.limitation: Almost every patient in these trials had progressed on palbociclib. What is being tested is therefore a second inhibitor after palbociclib rather than after ribociclib or abemaciclib. The two switch trials also differ in what their control arms received. One switched the endocrine partner in both arms, which isolates the inhibitor at the cost of making the answer one about a switched partner. The other held fulvestrant in both arms after progression on an aromatase inhibitor. Either way the control is endocrine monotherapy begun at progression, which performs poorly and makes superiority over it a low bar. The larger switch trial read its primary endpoint by investigator assessment. Central review of the same comparison returned a larger effect. The single-arm studies have no control at all. The resistance signature one of them proposes combines a retinoblastoma protein score, a cyclin E1 score and ESR1 status in a handful of tumours. That is a hypothesis about a biomarker rather than a test of one.
questions.next: If switching the inhibitor buys little, and if the endocrine partner was switched alongside it, what should that partner be once an aromatase inhibitor has failed?

questions.ask: What should the endocrine partner be once an aromatase inhibitor with a CDK4/6 inhibitor has failed?
questions.rationale: Oestrogen deprivation selects for ESR1 mutations that hold the receptor in an active conformation with no ligand bound. An aromatase inhibitor cannot reach a receptor that no longer needs its ligand. Fulvestrant can, but only at the exposure an intramuscular injection allows. An orally bioavailable degrader was meant to solve both problems at once.
questions.experiment: Randomised comparisons of an oral degrader against standard endocrine monotherapy, usually fulvestrant, in disease progressing after endocrine therapy. Three prespecified the ESR1-mutant population, called from plasma, alongside all patients. The third of those also randomised the degrader with and without a CDK4/6 inhibitor. One randomised two doses of a degrader against fulvestrant. Two tested a degrader against endocrine monotherapy with no mutation-defined population at all.
questions.finding: The first degrader to report lengthened progression-free survival against endocrine monotherapy in all patients, and by more in those whose disease carried an ESR1 mutation. The two later agents that prespecified the mutant population gained there and not in the population unselected for it. The agent randomised at two doses beat fulvestrant at both. The two tested with no mutation-defined population missed their primary endpoint. The degrader given with a CDK4/6 inhibitor beat the same degrader alone.
questions.limitation: Prior CDK4/6 inhibition was an entry requirement in only two of these trials. Elsewhere it was a stratification factor or nothing at all, which means these trials are not all describing the population this position describes. The comparator throughout is endocrine monotherapy in disease that has just progressed on endocrine therapy, where it performs poorly. That establishes superiority over a weak control rather than a rank order among the degraders, none of which has been compared with another. ESR1 status was read from circulating tumour DNA at each assay's own limit of detection. The mutant and wild-type groups are therefore set by a sequencing threshold rather than by a boundary in the biology. A tumour called wild-type may carry a subclone below it. The dose-ranging trial enrolled only postmenopausal patients and reported at a wider confidence convention than the phase III trials beside it. The trial that added a CDK4/6 inhibitor to a degrader admitted patients who had never had one, so that comparison does not settle the continuation question.
questions.next: If the receptor still drives only the part of this population whose receptor carries a mutation, what is driving the rest?

questions.ask: Does blocking the PI3K, AKT and mTOR axis restore endocrine sensitivity?
questions.rationale: This pathway is the best-documented route by which a hormone receptor-positive tumour keeps proliferating while its receptor is blocked. Activating PIK3CA mutations are common at diagnosis and are enriched under treatment. Loss of PTEN and activating AKT1 mutations reach the same node from other directions. Blocking the node should return the cell to depending on oestrogen.
questions.experiment: Randomised additions of an inhibitor to fulvestrant or exemestane at each level of the pathway: mTOR, PI3K-alpha, AKT, and PI3K with mTOR together. They differ in how the pathway alteration entered the design. One required it for entry. One prespecified the altered patients as a co-primary population inside an unselected trial. One reported a cohort defined by the absence of the alteration. Two ran a CDK4/6 inhibitor alongside, one of them in both arms and one in a third arm. A single-arm cohort took the alpha inhibitor into disease that had already progressed on a CDK4/6 inhibitor. A head-to-head comparison of two alpha inhibitors is running and has not reported.
questions.finding: The mTOR inhibitor, the alpha-selective inhibitor and the AKT inhibitor each lengthened progression-free survival over the endocrine partner alone. For the alpha-selective and the AKT inhibitors the gain was larger in tumours carrying a pathway alteration than in those without one. The dual PI3K and mTOR inhibitor produced the largest effect of any trial here. It produced it in a cohort selected for the absence of a PIK3CA mutation. Adding the alpha inhibitor to a CDK4/6 inhibitor and fulvestrant in the first line lengthened both progression-free and overall survival against those same two drugs. All of it is bought with hyperglycaemia, rash, stomatitis and diarrhoea, which decide how much of it a patient actually receives.
questions.limitation: Only two of these trials required progression on a CDK4/6 inhibitor. The mTOR and alpha-inhibitor trials were run before that class was routine. The AKT phase II trial enrolled nobody who had received one. The first-line triplet enrolled patients relapsing on adjuvant endocrine therapy, and its control arm carried a CDK4/6 inhibitor rather than endocrine therapy alone. Whether the genotype was an entry criterion, a co-primary population or a separately randomised cohort differs from trial to trial. That difference, rather than the drug, decides how much of each estimate is selection. Alterations were called on tumour tissue in some trials and on circulating tumour DNA in others. The two do not identify the same patients. The dual inhibitor's result is a wild-type cohort read at short follow-up against a fulvestrant control that did almost nothing, and its mutant cohort has not reported. The single-arm cohort that carried the alpha inhibitor into post-CDK4/6 disease has no control arm. Its report also carries a published expression of concern.
questions.next: If an alteration in this pathway is what makes a targeted addition worth giving, what should be done with the other alterations a sequencing report returns at progression?

questions.ask: Does an activating HER2 mutation found at progression change what to give?
questions.rationale: A small fraction of these tumours carry an activating mutation in ERBB2. The fraction rises after endocrine therapy. The mutation switches the receptor on without raising its copy number. Immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation therefore both report the tumour as HER2-negative. A receptor activated by mutation should still be blockable at its kinase.
questions.experiment: Cohorts inside basket studies gave a HER2 kinase inhibitor to patients whose tumours carried an activating HER2 mutation without amplification. One gave an irreversible inhibitor with fulvestrant and trastuzumab, and carried comparison arms of fulvestrant alone and of fulvestrant with trastuzumab. Another gave the same irreversible inhibitor with fulvestrant, in cohorts split by whether fulvestrant had already been given. A third paired a selective HER2 kinase inhibitor with trastuzumab, adding fulvestrant for hormone receptor-positive disease.
questions.finding: Responses occurred in each of these cohorts, in a population defined by the mutation rather than by amplification. In the study that carried comparison arms, neither fulvestrant alone nor fulvestrant with the antibody produced a response. That places the activity in the kinase inhibitor rather than in the endocrine partner. Clinical benefit appeared whether or not fulvestrant had been given before.
questions.limitation: These are small single-arm cohorts inside basket studies. Each gives an estimate of activity and no comparison against what a clinic would otherwise give. One of them reports its intervals at a wider confidence convention than the rest of this registry uses. They pool mutations in different domains of the receptor, which do not all respond alike. The mutation was called by whatever assay the enrolling centre happened to run. One cohort enrolled hormone receptor-positive and hormone receptor-negative disease together and gave fulvestrant only to the first group. It reports response in each group, but the receptor-negative group is a handful of patients. Another defines its cohorts by previous fulvestrant exposure rather than by line, which leaves how heavily pretreated its patients were unrecorded.
questions.next: If selecting on a genotype is what makes a small study work, what became of the resistance hypotheses that had no marker to select on?

questions.ask: Do the resistance mechanisms tested without a selecting biomarker give anything back?
questions.rationale: Not every proposed mechanism of endocrine resistance arrives with a marker to enrich for. Apoptotic priming through BCL2, mitotic dependence through Aurora A kinase, epigenetic silencing of the receptor, and the androgen receptor as an alternative nuclear receptor were each argued from laboratory work. Each named a drug that could be added to endocrine therapy, or given in its place, in disease that had already failed on endocrine therapy.
questions.experiment: Randomised additions to fulvestrant or exemestane after endocrine failure, two of them requiring failure on a CDK4/6 inhibitor as well. One trial randomised only whether fulvestrant was added to the experimental drug. Both of its arms therefore received that drug. Another randomised two doses of an androgen receptor agonist against each other, with no standard-therapy arm. The endpoints were clinical benefit rate, response rate or progression-free survival, with overall survival co-primary in only one.
questions.finding: No randomised comparison in this group beat its own control. Adding the BCL2 inhibitor to fulvestrant did not raise clinical benefit over fulvestrant alone. Adding the histone deacetylase inhibitor to exemestane moved neither progression-free survival nor overall survival. The Aurora A kinase trial found the same response rate with and without fulvestrant, which was the only thing it randomised. The androgen receptor agonist produced clinical benefit at both doses, with nothing but the other dose to read it against.
questions.limitation: Each of these is negative about the combination and the schedule it tested rather than about the mechanism, because none of them selected patients on the marker its own hypothesis names. The BCL2 trial's biomarker-defined subgroups were exploratory and small. The Aurora A trial leaves the activity of its own kinase inhibitor without a control anywhere in the trial. That signal is a single-arm observation. It also stratified on tumours with a very low oestrogen receptor level, so its population is broader than a hormone receptor-positive label suggests. The epigenetic trial enrolled mostly patients who had never had a CDK4/6 inhibitor, which makes it a test of reversing aromatase inhibitor resistance rather than resistance to the combination. The androgen trial assessed its primary endpoint only in patients whose androgen receptor positivity was confirmed centrally after randomisation. A quarter of those randomised fall outside that population.
questions.next: If nothing on offer restores dependence on the oestrogen receptor, when should endocrine-directed treatment be given up for cytotoxic treatment?

questions.ask: When should endocrine-directed treatment give way to chemotherapy or an antibody-drug conjugate?
questions.rationale: The convention is to hold cytotoxic treatment back while any endocrine option remains, because endocrine treatment is easier to live with. The convention assumes the remaining endocrine option still works. After a CDK4/6 inhibitor that is exactly what is in doubt. A conjugate was meant to move the threshold by delivering a cytotoxic payload only to cells carrying a surface antigen.
questions.experiment: Two trials randomised a CDK4/6 inhibitor with endocrine therapy against capecitabine in endocrine-resistant disease. Two more randomised a TROP2-directed conjugate against chemotherapy of the physician's choice, at different depths of prior chemotherapy. One asked whether adding a checkpoint inhibitor to such a conjugate helped. A single-arm study took a HER3-directed conjugate into disease that had had a CDK4/6 inhibitor and a line of chemotherapy. One ongoing trial moves the TROP2 conjugate ahead of the first chemotherapy line.
questions.finding: The two capecitabine trials disagree on progression-free survival. The disagreement follows their populations rather than their drugs. Neither of them produced an overall survival difference, which is the one thing they agree on. Both TROP2-directed conjugates lengthened progression-free survival against physician's choice chemotherapy. Only one of the two also lengthened overall survival. Adding a checkpoint inhibitor to a conjugate did not lengthen progression-free survival. The HER3-directed conjugate produced responses in a single arm.
questions.limitation: Neither capecitabine trial belongs to this position as it stands, because both gave a CDK4/6 inhibitor to patients who had never had one. They differ from each other in menopausal status and in how much of the population had had any treatment for metastatic disease, which is enough to explain the disagreement without invoking the drugs. Physician's choice names a different set of agents in each conjugate trial and in each country. The comparator is therefore not a fixed quantity across them. The two conjugate trials also sit at different depths of prior chemotherapy, which is the other reason their results are not interchangeable. A progression-free survival gain not followed by a gain in overall survival is a difference measured on imaging.
